TITLE: Giving Learners the Best of Both Worlds: Do Clinical Teachers Need to Guard Against Teaching Pattern Recognition to Novices?

ABSTRACT: The results support an additive model of clinical reasoning in which instructions to be feature oriented and to trust similarity improve performance in novice diagnosticians.

Teaching from the clinical reasoning literature:
combined reasoning strategies help novice
diagnosticians overcome misleading information
KEVIN WE VA,1 ROSE MH ATALA,2 VICKI RL EBLANC3 &L EE RB ROOKS4
OBJECTIVE Previous research has revealed a peda-
gogical beneﬁt of instructing novice diagnosticians to
utilise a combined approach to clinical reasoning
(familiarity-driven pattern recognition combined
with a careful consideration of the presenting fea-
tures) when diagnosing electrocardiograms (ECGs).
This paper reports 2 studies demonstrating that the
combined instructions are especially valuable in
helping students overcome biasing inﬂuences.
METHODS Undergraduate psychology students were
trained to diagnose 10 cardiac conditions via ECG
presentation. Half of all participants were instructed
to reason in a combined manner and half were
given no explicit instruction regarding the diagnostic
task. In Study 1 ( n = 60), half of each group was
biased towards an incorrect diagnosis through pre-
sentation of counter-indicative features. In Study 2
(n = 48), a third of the test ECGs were presented with
a correct diagnostic suggestion, a third with an
incorrect suggestion, and a third without a suggestion.
RESULTS Overall, the instruction to utilise a com-
bined reasoning approach resulted in greater diag-
nostic accuracy relative to leaving students to their
own intuitions regarding how best to approach
new cases. The effect was particularly pronounced
when cases were made challenging by biasing
participants towards an incorrect diagnosis, either
through mention of a speciﬁc feature or by making
an inaccurate diagnostic suggestion.
DISCUSSION These studies advance a growing
body of evidence suggesting that various diagnostic
strategies identiﬁed in the literature on clinical
reasoning are not mutually exclusive and that
trainees can beneﬁt from explicit guidance regard-
ing the value of both analytic and non-analytic
reasoning tendencies.

INTRODUCTION
Since the publication of Custers et al./C213s review 1 of
the clinical reasoning literature a decade ago, there
has been increasing recognition that, ﬁrstly, many of
the models of clinical reasoning present in the
medical education literature are not mutually
exclusive and, secondly, that there is value for the
diagnostician in not getting locked into any single
mode of thinking about clinical cases.
1,2 To a large
extent, the debate that has taken place in medical
education research is reﬂective of many broader
literatures aimed at understanding how humans
make decisions.
One approach to studying and ⁄ or understanding
judgement and decision making, commonly applied
in economics, is based upon a model of rationality,

the notion being that the utility of a decision can be
derived from the product of the value gained from
each particular outcome and the probability with
which the outcome will occur. From this analytical
perspective, it is an irrational act to buy a lottery
ticket because, although the pay-out to the winner
may be very large, the probability of winning is so
small that the resultant utility (the product of the 2
values) is less than the cost of the ticket.
3 In
medicine, severity and probability often interact in
the same manner, so that low-probability diagnoses
are intentionally considered because the cost of
missing a serious diagnosis would be signiﬁcant.
From this perspective, bias is deﬁned as a consistent
deviation from rationality. Psychologists Amos Tver-
sky and Daniel Kahneman, among others, provided
great insight into human judgement by systematically
identifying and experimentally exploring biases that
are prevalent in our decision making, work which
resulted in Kahneman receiving the Nobel Prize in
Economics in 2002. One such bias they identiﬁed is
the /C212availability heuristic /C213, which refers to the ten-
dency we have to base judgements on vivid or salient
outcomes (i.e. those that are readily /C212available/C213to us
when imagining what might happen and which,
thereby, seem more probable) rather than on a more
rational, utility-driven approach.
4 To follow up on
the above example, many continue to buy lottery
tickets despite the low utility of such actions because
the vividness and excitement generated through
imagining what it would be like to win contributes to
an over-estimation of the likelihood that one might
win. Importantly, these sorts of mental short-cuts
often (if not always) inﬂuence our decisions without
our being aware that the heuristic is being used,
thus leading many to argue that we can improve
medical decision making (or decision making more
generally) and reduce diagnostic errors by educating
individuals about the ways in which their decision
making can be biased.
5,6 Alternative, but comple-
mentary, strategies for achieving the same goal in
medicine include teaching individuals to become
better Bayesians by explicitly directing their attention
to the need to learn (and consider) the probability
of any particular diagnosis (and how that probability
is conditional upon the presence or absence of
variable signs and symptoms)
7 or by provision of
explicit diagnostic algorithms as guidance for how
to complete a diagnostic search.
8
An alternative view of decision making derives from
the argument that these biases exist with such
prevalence and robustness because they are useful
and, therefore, not something we should ever hope
to abolish from our decision making. Gerd Gigeren-
zer, among others, has noted that many of these
heuristics and their associated biases are adaptive;
they may leave us susceptible to error in some cases,
but, given our complicated world, they help us more
than they hurt.
9 We might have the illusion that
the use of heuristics is suboptimal, but that is because
their use is noticeable only in cases where the
heuristic leads to inaccurate decisions relative to what
might be deemed optimal by rational standards. By
analogy, in medical diagnosis, the use of pattern
recognition is often noticed, and labelled as prob-
lematic, when it has led to an incorrect diagnosis
based on superﬁcial similarity. A more complete
consideration, however, requires one to acknowledge
that pattern recognition strategies not only often
yield the same decision as analytic decision-making
tendencies, but they sometimes result in better
outcomes.
10 When a classic case of pneumonia
presents in a doctor /C213s ofﬁce, the features that could
be carefully collected and converted into a diagnosis
of pneumonia will share a great deal of overlap
Overview
What is already known on this subject
When teaching electrocardiogram diagnosis
there is pedagogical benefit in encouraging
students to utilise analytic and non-analytic
reasoning strategies rather than treating either
class of strategies solely as a source of
detrimental bias.
What this study adds
Maintaining an optimal balance between non-
analytic and analytic reasoning strategies is
fragile for students. Giving them explicit
instructions to utilise a combined approach to
reasoning helps them to overcome the diffi-
culty provided by mention of a counter-indic-
ative feature or an incorrect diagnosis, both of
which are legitimate instructional techniques.
Suggestions for further research
Further research should examine these phe-
nomena within non-visual diagnostic domains
and across varying levels of training and
experience.

with those of previously seen cases of pneumonia, so
assigning a diagnosis on either basis will yield the
same conclusion. Of real beneﬁt, however, is that the
concurrent reference to prior cases can overcome
some of the limitations of the traditionally recom-
mended careful, analytic inspection of features.
That is routinely considering the features in a very
careful, analytic manner may avoid the dangers of
premature closure, but it can also be detrimental.
Norman et al. have shown that prompting diagnosti-
cians to be particularly careful in their feature calls
can yield a list of features that is irreconcilable with
any particular diagnosis, possibly because considering
features individually rather than in context leads to
/C212overcalling/C213normal variants (i.e. leads to the diag-
nostician being misled by features that would not
have been distracting otherwise).
11 It is arguable
that, were that not the case, these sorts of non-
analytic decision-making tendencies would be much
more readily (and, in all likelihood, naturally)
extinguishable.
12
Taken together, these different views of our deci-
sion-making tendencies generate the impression
that balance between multiple decision-making ten-
dencies is necessary to enable a robust system that
will maximise diagnosticians /C213accuracy. In a recent
series of studies, we strived to test whether or not
there is pedagogical value in instructing novice
diagnosticians to avoid getting locked into any
single mode of reasoning. Absolute novices (under-
graduate psychology students) were given instruc-
tion in electrocardiogram (ECG) diagnosis. After a
training phase, we found that groups of participants
given advice to trust feelings of familiarity when
making their diagnoses but to also carefully consider
the features that are present on ECGs (i.e. those
who were instructed to use a /C212combined approach /C213
to clinical reasoning) revealed greater diagnostic
accuracy than groups of participants who were: (a)
given no advice regarding how to work through new
cases;
13 (b) were told to be analytic by adopting a
/C212feature-ﬁrst/C213approach to diagnosis in which all
features should be listed before generating a diag-
nosis; or (c) were told to be non-analytic by
instructing them simply to diagnose based on
familiarity-driven ﬁrst impressions of each new
ECG.
14 The combined instruction is not intended
(or expected) to have prompted a particular
reasoning process that could be used as a /C212how-to
guide/C213for diagnosticians, but, rather, was simply
aimed at helping trainees to beneﬁt from the
suggestion in the literature on clinical reasoning
that there are multiple mechanisms through which
one can accurately generate a diagnosis.
In the current paper we report on the ﬁndings from
a pair of additional studies aimed at testing the
robustness of this phenomenon. As alluded to
above, there are many ways that the diagnostic
process can go wrong. If he or she relies too
heavily on non-analytic processes (i.e. the feeling of
having seen it all before), the diagnostician may be
overly susceptible to missing key features that are
indicative of alternative diagnoses, but which do
not ﬁt the overall pattern of the case. If, by contrast,
the diagnostician relies too heavily on analytic
processes (i.e. being particularly systematic and
/C212objective/C213), his or her perception of the cohesive-
ness of the case may be undermined, thus resulting
in excessive weighting of unusual or distracting
features. One could easily expect that novices, who
have just learned a set of diagnostic rules, might be
especially vulnerable to this overly analytic ap-
proach. Here we report a pair of studies in which we
tried to make the case presentations particularly
difﬁcult by biasing participants /C213consideration of the
cases away from the correct diagnosis either through
mention of a feature consistent with an incorrect
diagnosis (Study 1) or through mention of a
plausible but incorrect diagnostic hypothesis (Study
2). These types of experimental manipulations are
consistent with the uncommon but important
sources of misinformation a clinician may obtain,
such as a referring doctor /C213s incorrect diagnosis or an
erroneous computer-generated list of ECG features.
In Study 1, the aim of the feature manipulation was
to induce people towards placing greater reliance
on their analytic tendencies (i.e. careful consider-
ation of the features presented in the case), whereas
the aim of the diagnostic hypothesis manipulation
in Study 2 was to induce people towards greater
reliance on their non-analytic tendencies (i.e.
greater inﬂuence of their Gestalt impressions).
Prior research by our group has shown the latter
manipulation to have a strong inﬂuence on the
diagnostic process.
15,16
METHODS
General methodology
Undergraduate psychology students were recruited
from McMaster University to ensure that participants
had no previous experience with ECG diagnosis.
They were given bonus credits in their introductory
psychology class for participation.
Both studies involved 3 phases (training, practice and
test) that took place in one-to-one teaching environ-

ments with a research assistant. Only the experimen-
tal manipulation during the test phase varied between
the 2 studies. During the training phase, the
researcher taught participants the basics regarding
ECG diagnosis (i.e. the names of the 12 leads and the
labels assigned to a normal waveform). They were
then taught the key features of 10 diagnostic
categories through presentation of a written feature
list and a series of examples. The diagnostic categories
were:
1 normal;
2 right ventricular hypertrophy;
3 left ventricular hypertrophy with strain;
4 left bundle branch block;
5 right bundle branch block;
6 acute anterior myocardial infarction;
7 acute inferior myocardial infarction;
8 ischaemia;
9 pericarditis, and
10 hyperkalaemia.
Within each category 4 examples were presented.
During presentation of the ﬁrst 2 examples, the
researcher pointed to and described the features that
made that particular ECG a member of the category.
During the presentation of the second 2 examples,
the participant was asked to do the same. This phase
of the experiment required 45–60 minutes to
complete per participant.
After studying all 10 categories in this way,
participants entered a practice phase during which
they were presented with a booklet of 10 ECGs,
all of which had been seen during training, but
which were randomly sorted without diagnostic
labels. At the start of the practice phase, partici-
pants were randomly assigned to either a /C212com-
bined instruction /C213group or a /C212no instruction /C213
group. Those in the combined instruction group
were encouraged to use a combination of analytic
and non-analytic reasoning strategies when con-
fronted with each new ECG through the following
instructions:
/C212New ECGs often look like ECGs that have been
seen before (i.e. during training). Trust this sense
of familiarity, but realise that basing decisions
solely on similarity can lead to diagnostic errors.
So, don/C213t ‘‘jump the gun’’. Consider the feature list
before providing a ﬁnal diagnosis. /C213
The other half of the participants were not given
instructions that would promote any particular
reasoning process. Instead, they were told:
/C212Assign a diagnosis to each ECG using whatever
strategy comes naturally to you. Feel free to use the
feature list, but approach each case using whatever
strategy seems most appropriate to help you
reach the correct diagnosis. /C213
All participants in both groups were allowed to view
the ECG, the feature list and the generic waveform
image from the training materials when assigning
their diagnosis. They were given feedback after
interpreting each ECG, consisting of the correct
diagnosis and an indication of which features
determined the correct diagnosis.
Finally, during the test phase, participants were
presented with an additional booklet of ECGs. All
participants were provided with the same instructions
and feature list as during the practice phase, but no
feedback was given regarding the accuracy of
performance during the test. The biasing interven-
tions were implemented during the test phase. No
time limits were imposed, but all participants
completed the entire study in 90–120 minutes.
Study-speciﬁc methodology
During the test phase of Study 1, participants were
presented with 1 of 2 possible test booklets, each
consisting of the same 16 ECGs. In 1 booklet the
ECGs were presented along with a distracting feature.
With each presentation, participants were asked to
consider (before trying to diagnose the ECG)
whether or not the feature named was present on the
recording. Participants were unaware that the feature
presented was indicative of an incorrect diagnosis
in all cases. However, in all cases it was somewhat
unclear whether or not the feature was actually
present. The other half of the participants were
shown the same set of 16 ECGs without an interfering
feature included. They were simply asked to provide a
diagnosis for each ECG using the instructions they
had been given in the practice phase of the study. In
other words, both instruction and bias were crossed,
between-subject, manipulations. The number of
correct diagnoses (out of 16) was calculated for each
participant and a 2-way
ANOVA was performed on this
accuracy variable with instruction and bias as
between-subject variables. Posthoc t-tests were used to
resolve the source of a signiﬁcant interaction.
The test phase of Study 2 was similar to that of Study
1 in that the biasing manipulation was implemented
during the test. In Study 2, however, the bias
condition was incorporated as a within-subjects
manipulation such that each participant was

presented with ECGs in each bias condition. Three
test booklets were used, each containing the same 18
ECGs, but differing in the information presented
along with the recording. Six of the ECGs were
presented with no additional information, 6 were
presented with the correct diagnosis, and 6 were
presented with an incorrect diagnosis. To avoid the
inﬂuence of prestige as much as possible, participants
were told that the diagnostic suggestion had been
raised by another psychology student at an equal level
of training. For example, 1 ECG was presented with
the statement: /C212This ECG was shown to a group of
psychology students and 1 of the diagnoses raised
was ischaemia. /C213Participants were then asked to
diagnose the ECG using the instructions they had
been given in the practice phase of the study. Adding
2 ECGs to the set used in Study 1 enabled us to
add a third bias condition while ensuring that each
ECG was presented equally often in each bias
condition by counter-balancing across participants.
The number of correct diagnoses (out of 6) within
each bias condition was calculated for each partici-
pant and a mixed design
ANOVA using instruction
(combined versus none) as a between-subjects factor,
and bias condition as a within-subjects factor was
performed on this accuracy variable. We also used
t-tests as planned comparisons, given that we did not
expect a difference across instruction within the
bias-correct condition.
RESULTS
Study 1
Sixty students participated in this experiment; 30
received combined instructions and 30 received no
reasoning instructions. Fifteen from each group
were given ECGs with an interfering feature and 15
were not.
ANOVA revealed a main effect of instruc-
tion; the group provided with the combined
reasoning instruction outperformed those given no
instruction on how to diagnose new ECGs
(F[1,56] = 9.06, P < 0.01). The main effect of bias
did not reach signiﬁcance, but was in the expected
direction ( F[1,56] = 1.87, P < 0.2). The interaction
between instruction and bias indicated that the
impact of a negatively biasing feature presentation
was greater in the no-instruction condition (effect
size = 1.02) than in the combined reasoning con-
dition (effect size = 0.32) ( F[1,56] = 3.7, P < 0.07).
t-tests further indicated that the accuracy rates
achieved when a biasing feature was presented were
lower than when no biasing feature was presented
in the no-instruction condition ( P < 0.06), but
that the accuracy rates did not differ in the
combined reasoning condition ( P > 0.6). The
mean scores for each condition are illustrated in
Table 1. All groups performed markedly better than
chance, which would result in a score of 1.6 ⁄ 16
given that there were 10 possible response
categories.
Study 2
A total of 48 students participated in this experi-
ment; 24 received combined instructions and 24
received no reasoning instructions. All participants
were presented with 6 ECGs in each of the bias
conditions (correct diagnosis, incorrect diagnosis,
no bias).
ANOVA revealed that none of the main
effects of instruction, bias or the bias · instruction
interactions were statistically signiﬁcant. Planned
comparisons revealed, however, that the key com-
parison (combined versus no-instruction within the
bias-incorrect condition) revealed a statistically
signiﬁcant difference ( F[1,46] = 4.2, P < 0.05).
Similarly, although the group given combined
instructions did not reveal a statistically signiﬁcant
effect of bias ( F[2,46] = 1.4, P > 0.25), there was
a signiﬁcant difference between the bias-incorrect
condition and the bias-correct condition in the
no-instruction group ( F[1,46] = 4.3, P < 0.05). The
mean scores for each condition are illustrated in
Table 2. Again, all groups performed markedly
better than chance, which would result in a score
of 0.6 ⁄ 6 given that there were 10 possible response
categories.

DISCUSSION
This pair of studies provides further empirical
support for the notion that explicitly telling novice
diagnosticians to utilise multiple forms of reasoning
(in this case, familiarity-driven pattern recognition
combined with careful consideration of the present-
ing features) can result in improved diagnostic
accuracy. Despite the intuitive nature of statements
such as /C212no single tool will be right for every job /C213,a
series of studies, including these, has now been
conducted that suggest students do not spontane-
ously adopt this approach to clinical reasoning as
effectively as they might.
11,13,14 In other words, there
appears to be pedagogical beneﬁt in explicitly guid-
ing students to reason in a way that probably sounds
as if it should occur naturally. Although nobody can
control (or even say with certainty) what reasoning
processes are operational when a diagnostician works
through a case, there is every reason to believe that
participants in the no-instruction condition would
have been inﬂuenced by similarity when making their
diagnostic decisions
13,17 and it is inconceivable that
they would not have utilised the feature list to help
scan each ECG for features. However, participants in
that group did not perform as successfully as partic-
ipants who had been explicitly told to trust feelings of
familiarity and to be careful not to overlook pre-
senting features.
Unique to this study are ﬁndings that suggest just
how frail this balance between analytic and non-
analytic reasoning strategies can be and that instruc-
tion to adopt a combined reasoning approach can
help maintain this balance when faced with chal-
lenging cases. Biasing participants either towards
excessive reliance on feature-level information (as
might occur if one were overly analytic) or towards
excessive reliance on diagnosis-level information (as
might occur if one were overly non-analytic) had the
impact of reducing diagnostic accuracy differentially
across groups of participants. In both studies, those
randomly assigned to receive a combined reasoning
instruction showed no decline in performance when
they were intentionally misled by the researcher
towards an incorrect response, by contrast with those
who were not given any instruction about how to
reason through these stimuli. Study 2 is the ﬁrst study
in 6 not to have shown an overall main effect of
combined reasoning instructions compared with
other reasoning instructions,
11,13,14 a fact that leads
us to suspect that performance in the no-bias
condition for this group was simply anomalously
(and erroneously) low.
Limitations of this programme of research include
the fact that it is intentionally focused narrowly on
knowledge-based components of the diagnostic pro-
cess in an aim to better understand how knowledge is
organised in memory and how it can best be utilised
in practice. We intentionally use visual materials
(ECGs) in order to study the balance between
analytic and non-analytic processing. There are
certainly other aspects of practice that deﬁne com-
petence for doctors, including the related, but
under-studied, aspect of making treatment decisions,
and broader tendencies that are usually described
as being non-cognitive (e.g. communication skills or
the inclination towards re-investing one /C213s extra
mental resources into continuing professional or
personal development).
18 In addition, it remains to
be seen whether or not the effects reported in this
paper will generalise to other medical training
contexts with actual medical trainees. Absolute nov-
ices were selected for this research to ensure naı ¨vete´
with respect to ECG diagnosis, thus maximising the
control we had over prior relevant experiences and
minimising the mental database of previously seen
ECGs on which participants could draw. Whether or
not these strategies yield similar (and longterm)

beneﬁts for medical students at intermediate or

foot, at least in visual domains such as those provided

As we mentioned earlier, we stress that we do not
interpret these ﬁndings to mean that we have
discovered the process through which to maximise
diagnostic success. On the contrary, among the
principles guiding this work is the notion that
diagnostic ability is somewhat amorphous and ﬂexi-
ble.
2 Better diagnosticians are likely to be those who
can overcome case-speciﬁc weaknesses through the
recruitment of additional diagnostic strategies
(either consciously or unconsciously) as it is unlikely
that any single diagnostic pathway will be capable
of resolving every patient presentation a doctor is
likely to encounter. Better diagnosticians may also be
those who are less likely to be satisﬁed (again, either
consciously or unconsciously) with diagnoses that
are derived from a single diagnostic pathway because
these ﬁndings and the work that precedes them
suggest that increased reliance on any single diag-
nostic strategy is likely to harm performance. Further
work is required, however, to tease apart the rela-
tionships between these phenomena and ability. For
now, we treat these ﬁndings as simply indicative of
the value that can be derived from providing explicit
guidance regarding appropriate ways to solve diag-
nostic problems without limiting that guidance to any
single particular strategy.

The beneﬁts of ﬂexibility: the pedagogical value of
instructions to adopt multifaceted diagnostic
reasoning strategies
Tavinder K Ark, Lee R Brooks & Kevin W Eva
OBJECTIVES Building on the advice of previous
research to avoid parsing diagnostic strategies too
ﬁnely, recent studies have shown that teaching
novices to utilise analytic and non-analytic reasoning
strategies yields higher diagnostic accuracy than
teaching either in isolation. This study assesses the
extent to which students spontaneously adopt a
combined approach and compares its beneﬁts with
those experienced with a contrastive learning strategy
known to enhance analogical transfer.
METHODS A sample of 48 naı ¨ve students were
trained to identify features on electrocardiograms
(ECGs) and assign diagnoses. Half the participants
learned in a standard manner, encountering diag-
noses (and their associated features) in sequence.
The remaining participants were explicitly instructed
to draw comparisons between the diagnostic category
being learned and another confusable diagnostic
category (contrastive learning). Half the participants
in both groups were further instructed to carefully
identify all features while trusting guidance provided
by feelings of familiarity (a combined reasoning
strategy). The remaining participants were given
no instructions on how to approach the diagnostic
task.
RESULTS Greater diagnostic accuracy was achieved
following both contrastive learning and instructions
to use a combined reasoning strategy relative to the
control conditions. These variables did not interact
with each other, nor did they interact with novelty of
the test case. The effects were observed immediately
after learning and following a 1-week delay.
DISCUSSION The results emphasise the importance
of explicitly empowering students to utilise multiple
diagnostic strategies, including non-analytic approa-
ches. In addition, this study reveals the beneﬁt that
can be gained from contrastive learning in a medical
domain.

INTRODUCTION
One of the ongoing debates in medical education
focuses upon the extent to which various models of
diagnostic decision-making best characterise the
diagnostic expertise of doctors.
1 The goal is to
capture the essence of expertise in a manner that can
be taught to novices, thus increasing the efﬁciency
with which they become experts. This work began in
the 1970s with Elstein et al.’s presentation of the
hypothetico-deductive model of reasoning
2 and
quickly evolved into a plethora of competing theories.
Reviews of clinical reasoning began to be published
as early as 1996.
3 The conclusion of Custers et al.’s
review was that many forms of knowledge are avail-
able to clinicians and, as a result, attempts to
determine how various forms of knowledge are
co-ordinated during diagnosis are more likely to
yield dividends than attempts to prove any single
framework correct.
3

Multiple studies have supported this contention, as
does the overwhelmingly robust phenomenon of
context speciﬁcity, but only recently has anyone
begun to experimentally test the practical implica-
tions of a /C212combined/C213, /C212ﬂexible/C213or /C212multifaceted/C213
model of clinical reasoning.
4 Building on the work of
Norman et al.,5 Ark et al.6 tested the efﬁcacy of
a variety of instructions provided to novice readers of
electrocardiograms (ECGs). An analytic (i.e. /C212feature
ﬁrst/C213) strategy was promoted by stressing the import-
ance of carefully considering the features present on
an ECG before considering potential diagnoses. That
is, participants were instructed to approach the task
of ECG diagnosis in a systematic and controlled
manner. By contrast, other participants were
encouraged to use a non-analytic (i.e. /C212ﬁrst impres-
sion/C213) strategy in that they were instructed simply to
trust feelings of familiarity given that a presenting
ECG might appear similar to other ECGs that had
been seen during training. Another group of partic-
ipants was given both sets of instructions (i.e. to
adopt a /C212combined/C213strategy of trusting familiarity
while double checking ﬁrst impressions by carefully
considering the features). When tested, participants
given either set of non-combined instructions
demonstrated equal diagnostic accuracy, but their
performance was poor compared with that of
participants who had been given a combined
instruction. This was true for each of the 3 distinct
ways the combined reasoning strategy was
operationalised (i.e. regardless of whether the
instruction to systematically consider the features
presented in a case was given simultaneously or
sequentially with the instruction to use familiarity, or
whether the instruction to utilise familiarity was given
explicitly or implicitly).
Still at issue, however, is whether or not promoting
a co-ordinated approach (i.e. a combined strategy)
to diagnostic decision making actually improves
performance. One could justiﬁably argue that
trainees would naturally and spontaneously adopt a
combined approach to diagnostic reasoning and that
the differences observed by Ark et al.
6 were due to
the detrimental impact of prompting participants to
use one or the other strategy in isolation. To truly
determine whether or not an explicit instruction to
utilise a combined strategy is beneﬁcial requires an
additional control group of participants who are left
to their own devices – a group of participants who are
instructed to adopt freely whatever diagnostic strategy
seems most reasonable given the categorisation
scheme they are trying to learn. The need to assess
such a comparison provided the ﬁrst objective of this
study.
The second objective was to compare the magnitude
of beneﬁt of an instruction to use a combined
reasoning strategy with that of another strategy that
has proven successful in increasing the rate of
analogical transfer in non-medical domains. Analo-
gical transfer is deﬁned by psychologists as successful
problem solving through the use of solution
principles that were learned in response to problems
encountered previously.
7 That is, solutions are
transferred from one problem to another by way of
analogy. For example, learning the role that acid-base
balance plays in a particular clinical context can
provide a useful analogy to help one understand the
physiological mechanism associated with another
clinical presentation dependent on homeostasis.
That being said, the rate at which transfer occurs
tends to be counter-intuitively low, a phenomenon
that has been argued to be a root cause of context
speciﬁcity.
8 Moreover, studies have shown that simply
stating the solution principles and providing exam-
ples is insufﬁcient to help learners apply the princi-
ples when trying to solve new cases.
9,10 Many learning

Overview
What is already known on this subject
Various models of diagnostic reasoning have
found support in the literature as hallmarks of
expertise, but these models need not be
considered mutually exclusive.
What this study adds
Evidence that an explicit instruction to utilise
both analytic and non-analytic forms of diag-
nostic reasoning can improve novice clini-
cians’ diagnostic accuracy beyond that
achieved by the spontaneous approaches they
adopt without such an explicit instruction.
Suggestions for further research
Future research might determine which sti-
mulus-based and diagnostician-based factors
lead clinicians to adopt a less than optimally
balanced approach to clinical reasoning, when
such factors increase the rate of diagnostic
errors, and whether or not particular actions
might help diagnosticians maintain a balanced
approach.

strategies have been identiﬁed that can improve rates
of transfer, but the generalisability of many of these
ﬁndings to the ﬁeld of medicine has yet to be tested.
In other domains contrastive learning has arguably
been shown to be the most successful strategy for
enhancing transfer rates in problem solvers and it is
certainly among the most extensively studied
strategies.
11–13 Contrastive learning involves
prompting the learner to explicitly search for
similarities and differences between problems. Doing
so, it is thought, enables students to better avoid
being distracted by the superﬁcial surface elements of
problems (e.g. the speciﬁc clinical presentation) by
helping them understand the underlying deep
structure (e.g. the pathophysiology of the disease)
that enables the solution principle to be applied
across variable problems. Although some would
argue that true analogical transfer can only succeed
by virtue of making a comparison across the deep
structural level of problems, it is plausible that
promotion of a contrastive learning style would also
help students in tasks like ECG diagnosis by assisting
them to learn the critical features that discriminate
between categories. That is, highlighting the similar-
ities and differences between disorders in terms of
the features present on an ECG might make the
diagnosticity of each symptom more apparent or
more inﬂuential in helping students learn to
discriminate between categories. Hatala et al.
14 have
already demonstrated the value of /C212mixed practice /C213.
After learning the basics of ECG interpretation,
participants in their study had the opportunity to
practise ECG diagnosis via the presentation of ECGs
that had not been sorted into disorders, but were
mixed across the various diagnoses.
14 The current
study extends these ﬁndings by testing the value of
implementing a contrastive learning approach during
the initial learning of the categorisation scheme.
Participants in the contrastive learning condition
were asked to explicitly compare diagnostic
categories that were:
1 similar by virtue of their having features in
common, and
2 known to be easily confusable based on the results
of previous studies.
For example, participants were asked to compare and
contrast the features of ischaemia with those of left
ventricular hypertrophy with strain; both share S )T
depression and T wave inversions in many of the
leads on an ECG. This instructional manipulation was
contrasted with a non-contrastive condition in which
normal practices were applied: participants were
asked to learn the features of a series of diseases in
sequence, as they would when working through most
courses and textbooks.
15
In summary, half the participants were asked to study
the ECG features present in a series of cardiologic
disorders without explicit reference being made to the
value of comparing and contrasting any particular
disorder with another (i.e. the non-contrastive learn-
ing condition). The other half of the participants were
asked to learn the disorders in the same sequence, but
learners were told to intentionally consider the
similarities and differences between pairs of disorders
(i.e. the contrastive learning condition). Within each
of these groups, half the participants were instructed
to trust any sense of familiarity they might have when
diagnosing test cases while also carefully considering
features (i.e. the combined reasoning condition),
whereas the other half were given no instructions
regarding how best to approach the diagnosis of test
cases (i.e. the spontaneous reasoning condition). If
learners tend spontaneously to utilise a combined
approach successfully, then explicit instructions to
adopt this approach would be expected to have
minimal effect. Any differences observed across these
2 variables would, however, provide a pedagogic
strategy to enable implementation of the literatures
on clinical reasoning and analogical transfer in
clinical teaching contexts.
METHODS
Participants
A sample of 48 undergraduate psychology students
enrolled at McMaster University participated in this
3-phase experiment for course credit. None of the
participants had previous experience with ECGs.
Design and procedure
Training phase
Using the material developed by Norman et al.,
5 all
participants were taught general information
regarding the 12 leads in an ECG during one-to-one
teaching sessions with the experimenter. They were
then taught to recognise the general structures of
a normal ECG waveform (i.e. P wave, QRS complex,
S)T segment and T wave).
After this introduction participants were randomly
assigned to 1 of 2 learning conditions. Those in the
283

non-contrastive condition were taught each of 8
diagnostic categories, beginning with normal, using
a feature list containing the key features for each
diagnosis. For example, right bundle branch block
was presented as typically having:
• RSR (rabbit ears) present in V1 and V2, and
• a widened QRS complex.
16
For each diagnostic category, participants were pre-
sented with 4 examples. For the ﬁrst 2 ECGs in each
category, the instructor identiﬁed key features that
were indicative of that particular disorder using the
feature list. For the latter 2, participants were asked to
identify the relevant features before moving onto the
next diagnostic category. This process was repeated
until all diagnostic categories and their examples
were presented. On average, this learning task
required approximately 35 minutes to complete.
The procedure for participants assigned to the
contrastive learning condition was identical, with
the exception that, instead of merely identifying the
features, participants were asked to compare and
contrast the features present on each example with
those of a normal ECG and with those of
a confusable differential. For example, participants
were asked to compare and contrast the ﬁrst 2 slides
in the set of 4 examples of left ventricular hyper-
trophy with those of a normal ECG by identifying
features that were similar and dissimilar. They were
then asked to compare and contrast the latter 2
examples with 2 examples of ischaemia (a disorder
that was known to be confusable, given our prior
work). Participants were encouraged to self-generate
the similarities and differences between categories
as much as possible. However, in instances where
they failed, the instructor would provide hints at the
differences. This process was repeated until all
diagnostic categories had been considered. On
average, training time for participants in the
contrastive learning condition was 5–10 minutes
longer than that in the non-contrastive learning
condition.
Immediate test phase
After the training phase, participants were presented
with a booklet consisting of 7 ECGs that had been
randomly selected from the training materials.
During this phase, participants were randomly
further divided into 1 of 2 reasoning conditions.
To emphasise a combined diagnostic strategy, half
the participants were given the following instructions,
which were intended to emphasise the value of both
analytic and non-analytic approaches (i.e. combined
instructions) to medical diagnosis:
/C212For each ECG, assign a diagnosis using similarity as
a guide. New ECGs often look like ECGs that have
been seen before (i.e. during training). Trust this
sense of familiarity, but realise that basing decisions
solely on similarity can lead to diagnostic errors.
So, don/C213t jump the gun. Use the response sheet list
to indicate the features that can be seen. Use the
disease list to help you.’
By contrast, participants in the spontaneous reason-
ing condition were told to:
/C212Assign a diagnosis to each ECG using whatever
strategy comes naturally to you. Feel free to use the
feature list, but approach each case using whatever
strategy seems most appropriate to help you reach
the correct diagnosis. /C213
All participants were allowed to view the ECG when
assigning their diagnosis. They were told the correct
answer after diagnosing each ECG. Whenever an
incorrect diagnosis was assigned, immediate feedback
was given that reinforced the instructions that had
been provided.
Delayed test phase
One week after training, participants were presented
with a booklet of 15 ECGs; 8 were novel and 7 had
been seen during training but were distinct from the
ECGs seen during the immediate test phase. Partic-
ipants were given the same reasoning instructions as
those they had received during the immediate test
phase and were asked to diagnose each ECG. Feed-
back was not provided during this phase of the
experiment.

Feature identiﬁcation
Previous work has suggested that a combined
reasoning approach to ECG diagnosis results in
better performance relative to when trainees are
instructed to be very analytic due to a decrease in the
diagnostician’s tendency to be distracted by mislead-
ing features.
5,6 The feature data in this study, how-
ever, were not analysed as a function of reasoning
instruction because it is impossible to know which
features the spontaneous reasoning group identiﬁed
as participants in that group were not instructed to
record the features they considered. This was to avoid
biasing their spontaneous approach to reasoning, but
it makes any feature comparison across reasoning
conditions meaningless.
The feature data provided by the combined reason-
ing group were analysed as a function of learning
condition for the sake of completeness, but there was
no a priori reason to expect a difference between
contrastive and non-contrastive learning conditions
on this variable. For each ECG, features were
categorised as:
1 hit-indicative (a feature that was present and
indicative of the correct diagnosis);
2 hit-not indicative (a feature that was present but
indicative of another diagnosis), or
3 false alarm (a feature that was not present in the
ECG).

feature-oriented and to trust similarity-based reason-

performance than alternative sets of instructions.
Prior work compared instructions to use a combined
reasoning strategy with instructions to use either of
this strategy’s components in isolation, and found the
combined reasoning strategy to be superior. This
study adds a comparison with the natural tendencies
of novice diagnosticians, thus conﬁrming that,
indeed, instructions to utilise a combined reasoning
strategy can improve performance above and beyond
what can be expected in the absence of such
instructions. However, based on these results, we
cannot make conclusive statements about whether
participants in the spontaneous reasoning condition
did or did not implement a combined reasoning
strategy or whether they did so but less effectively.
Our suspicion is the latter. The consistency with
which /C212old/C213(i.e. previously seen) ECGs were diag-
nosed more accurately than /C212new/C213ECGs suggests that
similarity-based processes were operational in all
conditions, although past work leads us to assume
these processes were applied unconsciously in many
instances. Moreover, it is implausible that
participants would exert no effort in trying carefully
to consider the features present on an ECG and
match them to the possible diagnostic categories,
given that the diagnostic categories were deﬁned
during training based upon the features, and that all
participants had a feature list available to them when
making their diagnoses. Thus, despite the likelihood
that some form of combined reasoning will be
adopted spontaneously by diagnosticians, the
provision of explicit and concrete instructions
regarding how to do so appears to be beneﬁcial.
In addition, this study revealed that learners who were
instructed to compare and contrast categories (those
in the contrastive condition) achieved greater diag-
nostic accuracy than those who were simply told to
learn the relationship between the features and
disorders (those in the non-contrastive condition).
One plausible, although speculative, explanation for
this ﬁnding is that participants in the contrastive
condition better understood the diagnosticity of each
symptom. That is, they were less likely to fall victim to
premature closure due to an increased awareness that
a feature indicative of a particular disorder can also be
indicative of another diagnosis. Whether or not this
mechanism provides the best explanation for these
ﬁndings requires further study. Nevertheless, it
appears safe to conclude that the beneﬁts of
contrastive learning (relative to the more traditional
non-contrastive approach to learning) that have been
found in the psychology literature on transfer do
generalise to the domain of medicine (at least with
highly visual tasks like ECG diagnosis). Moreover, it
appears to be equally effective relative to the strategy of
instructing learners to adopt a combined reasoning
approach. However, it should be noted that although
participants in the contrastive learning condition
spent slightly more time studying the material than
participants in the non-contrastive learning condition,
no such time-on-task differences confound the com-
parisons of combined versus spontaneous instructions.
It is worth emphasising that the conclusion that
contrastive learning and combined reasoning
instructions hold pedagogical value applies readily to
the most ecologically valuable condition – the pres-
entation of novel ECGs after a time delay. These
instructions enabled 70% accuracy even when ECGs
that had never been seen before were presented to
participants a full week after their initial training
(Table 2, novel ECGs). It is also worth noting that
comparison of the other half of Table 2 (previously
seen ECGs) with the results of the immediate test
condition illustrated in Table 1 (in which all ECGs
were previously seen yet unique from the delayed test
ECGs) provides further evidence for the beneﬁt of
prior experience with speciﬁc cases. Little decline in
accuracy was observed over the course of the week for
ECGs that had been seen before, especially in
comparison with the magnitude of the difference
between previously seen and novel ECGs.
Limitations of this study include the fact that only 1
diagnostic domain (ECG), a highly visual domain at
that, was utilised and that our participants were
undergraduate psychology students as opposed to
medical trainees. In fact, we view the latter limitation
as a strength of the study design in the context of this

absolute novices with no prior ECG experience. The

6,17 A second
limitation of this study is its small sample size.
However, the sample size was clearly large enough for
the analyses to hold sufﬁcient power to reveal
statistically signiﬁcant differences between groups.
In conclusion, it appears that instructions to use
contrastive learning and instructions to use
combined reasoning lead to signiﬁcantly higher
diagnostic accuracy than instructions for non-
contrastive learning and student-derived reasoning
strategies, respectively. Students might naturally
utilise a combined reasoning strategy, but they appear
to do so with less beneﬁt than when they are provided
with concrete instructions regarding how to approach
the diagnostic task. Therefore, prompting novices to
consider the similarities and differences between
diagnostic categories (perhaps especially those that
are likely to form a differential diagnosis) and
providing them with explicit instructions to utilise
a combined reasoning strategy appears to represent
an effective pedagogic suggestion that can aid in the
education of novices and facilitate their progress to
a more expert level of diagnostic capability.

Fostering diagnostic knowledge through computer-
supported, case-based worked examples: effects of
erroneous examples and feedback
Veronika Kopp, 1 Robin Stark 2 & Martin R Fischer 1
OBJECTIVES A case-based, worked example approach
was realised in a computer-based learning environ-
ment with the intention of facilitating medical
students/C213diagnostic knowledge. In order to enhance
the effectiveness of the approach, two additional
measures were implemented: erroneous examples
and elaborated feedback. In the context of an
experimental study, the two measures were varied
experimentally.
METHODS A total of 153 medical students were ran-
domly assigned to four experimental conditions of a
2 · 2-factor design (errors versus no errors, elabo-
rated feedback versus knowledge of correct result
[KCR]). In order to verify the sustainability of the
effects, a subgroup of subjects ( n = 52) was compared
with a control group of students who did not
participate in the experiment ( n = 145) on a regular
multiple-choice question (MCQ) test.
RESULTS Results show that the acquisition of diag-
nostic knowledge is mainly supported by providing
erroneous examples in combination with elaborated
feedback. These effects were independent from
differences in time-on-task and prior knowledge.
Furthermore, the effects of the learning environment
proved sustainable.
CONCLUSIONS Our results demonstrate that the
case-based, worked example approach is effective
and efﬁcient.

INTRODUCTION
Diagnosing is a fundamental competence for every
doctor. However, students and attending doctors
have difﬁculties ascertaining the right diagnosis.
Gra¨sel and Mandl,
1 for example, showed that medical
students at the end of their clinical studies proceed
in an additive and mechanistic way; they tend to
collect large amounts of data without building
concrete hypotheses. We postulate that the diagnostic
knowledge base of the students encompassing
declarative knowledge components (conceptual
knowledge: /C212what information /C213) and action-related
knowledge components like strategic knowledge
(/C212how information /C213
2) and teleological knowledge
(/C212why information /C2132) is deﬁcient. Furthermore,
these components are not sufﬁciently integrated
into more abstract structures (schemata) which would
allow effective and efﬁcient diagnostic reasoning.
In order to overcome this problem and to foster
diagnostic knowledge which allows competent diag-
nostic reasoning, a complex computer-based learning
environment was developed based on the CASUS
TM
online learning tool, which has proved effective in
various studies.
3,4
Following Mandin, 5 diagnostic reasoning can be
understood as schema-based problem-solving.
Therefore, effective learning environments that
systematically support students in constructing and
organising schemata must be provided. We postulate
that learning environments taking advantage of the

achieve this instructional goal. Learning with worked
examples is superior to directly teaching abstract
principles, as well as to actively solving training
problems – at least with regard to initial skill
acquisition.
6 This worked example effect is attributed
to the fact that studying worked examples imposes
lower levels of cognitive load on the learner than
solving training problems, particularly because no
extensive search processes with regard to the correct
solution steps are involved.
6 Therefore, more cogni-
tive resources can be invested in processes of schema
construction. Moreover, studying worked examples
(by contrast with attempting to solve training prob-
lems) focuses the learner /C213s attention on information
that is relevant to schema construction. In various
domains /C212schema-based problem solving is consid-
ered to be very efﬁcient and therefore often seen as a
marking feature of experts /C213problem solving /C213.
6
However, studies on the self-explanation effect8–11
clearly show that studying worked examples does not
automatically result in effective problem-solving
schemas. In order to achieve this goal, cognitive and
meta-cognitive self-explanation processes have to be
fostered systematically by implementing additional
instructional measures.
11–13 In addition, the worked
example method has to be adapted to the instruc-
tional context, instructional goals and domain in
which it is implemented.
So far, worked examples have been investigated
primarily in studies on initial learning in rather
simple and well-structured domains. Thus, we com-
bined the example method with elements of case-
based learning which proved effective in various
problem-based learning scenarios in medicine.
14,15 In
addition, two instructional measures aimed at foster-
ing diagnostic knowledge by stimulating processes of
schema induction were integrated into the learning
environment: erroneous worked examples and
feedback.
A major objective of our study was to assess the
effectiveness of erroneous examples and feedback in
the context of our case-based, worked example
approach. Furthermore, the sustainability of the
learning environment in general was investigated.
Learning from errors
Confronting learners with errors introduces difﬁcul-
ties for the learner – difﬁculties which are desirable
because they can foster the quality of learning
processes and, as a result, learning outcomes.
16 The
method represents a particularly promising measure in
the ﬁeld of medicine, where errors in the process of
diagnosing can have fatal consequences.
17 Following
the classiﬁcation of diagnostic errors by Graber et al.,18
we focused on relevant and severe cognitive errors
caused by /C212inadequate knowledge or faulty data gath-
ering, inaccurate clinical reasoning, or faulty veriﬁca-
tion/C213.
18 Oser and Spychiger 19 assume that every error
can be learned from when and if learners use the error
purposefully as such an opportunity. Therefore,
learners must identify the error and understand the
correct solution by systematically comparing the
incorrect solution with the correct one. A study by
Grosse and Renkl
20 on learning from worked examples
can be interpreted in terms of the necessity of
implementing effective feedback methods when
confronting learners with erroneous examples.

What this study adds

Time-on-task
The implementation of erroneous examples and
feedback in the present study aimed to enhance the
effectiveness of the learning environment by fostering
the quality of learning processes. However, coping with
erroneous examples and processing elaborated feed-
back information (or compensating superﬁcial feed-
back by self-explanation behaviour) and the resulting
processes can prolong the time-on-task, thereby
confounding the quality and quantity of learning
processes. From a practical perspective, such effects
are acceptable when the prolonging is moderate and
at the same time associated with substantial learning
effects. However, from a theoretical perspective, these
effects are only acceptable when they do not under-
mine the internal validity of the study. Despite these
potential problems, time-on-task was not restricted
because of considerations about ecological validity:
following an integrative research approach,
27 we planned
to investigate the effects of the two instructional
measures under conditions which are not too far from
realistic learning scenarios in practice.
Research questions
1 To what extent is time-on-task increased by
erroneous examples and feedback?
We expected both measures to increase time-on-task.
However, we postulated that the potential effects on
diagnostic knowledge cannot be explained by
differences in time-on-task.
2 To what extent is diagnostic knowledge facilitated
by erroneous examples and feedback?
We assumed that both erroneous examples and
elaborated feedback have positive effects on the
acquisition of diagnostic knowledge and that the
combination of both measures is especially effective.
3 To what extent are effects of the learning environ-
ment sustainable?
We supposed that effects of the learning environment
on conceptual knowledge would still be veriﬁable
6 weeks after the learning session.
METHODS
Sample and design
A total of 153 medical students (104 women, 49 men)
from two Munich medical faculties, Germany, took
part in the study. All participants were engaged in
clinical studies and were in the second to the sixth
clinical semesters. The average age was around
25 years (mean = 25.02 years, standard deviation
[SD] = 3.62). Students were voluntarily recruited and
received €40 for participation. The subjects were
randomly assigned to the four conditions of a
2 · 2-factor design (Table 1).
Sustainability was assessed with students in their
second clinical semester. Arterial hypertension is part
of the curriculum during this semester and is also
part of a regular multiple-choice question (MCQ)
test. From this population, we drew a sample of
students who had participated in our study ( n = 52;
experimental group) and compared their results on
the MCQ test with those of the rest of the students
from the second clinical semester ( n = 145; control
group). Experimental and control group subjects did
not differ in terms of relevant learning prerequisites.
Furthermore, experimental group students did not
differ from the rest of the students, who participated
in the main study but not in the sustainability study,
with respect to relevant learning prerequisites and
diagnostic knowledge.
Learning environment
The learning environment, integrated in the
CASUS learning tool, consisted of a schema

learners see themselves in the role of a student on
an elective working together with a general practi-
tioner (GP) who gives feedback. All examples begin
with a clinical situation. The (ﬁctitious) student
starts drawing his conclusions for the working
diagnosis and for the further workup. Subsequently,
the GP gives feedback on his diagnostic steps. The
sequence of giving information, drawing conclu-
sions and obtaining feedback then continues until
the ﬁnal diagnosis is reached. Every example
consists of three or four such sequences containing
three or four screenshots.
The additional schema allows the steps of the
diagnostic process to be contextualised by providing
structured information on all secondary hypertension
diseases. Additionally, the schema explains the
relationship between the different illnesses and the
underlying pathophysiological processes. Further-
more, it indicates which further information is
needed for excluding and including diagnoses,
respectively.
Instructional measures
Errors
In the condition without errors, the student comes to
the right considerations on the basis of the given
information, draws the right conclusions and ﬁnishes
the case with the right diagnosis. In the condition
with errors, the student makes several severe errors.
The choice of errors was guided by the error
taxonomy described by Graber et al.,
18 as well as by an
analysis of relevant cognitive errors in this domain.
After each erroneous decision, the error is corrected
in the GP /C213s feedback.
Feedback
In the elaborated version of the feedback, the
(ﬁctitious) doctor gives additional explanations to
the (right or wrong) considerations and further
consequences drawn by the student. Furthermore,
he elucidates the diagnostic process referring to
underlying pathophysiological knowledge. The con-
ditions with the KCR feedback were very frugal in
comparison with the elaborated version. Consider-
ations, conclusions and further procedures are eval-
uated only as right or wrong; no further explanation
is forthcoming. In the condition /C212errors and KCR
feedback/C213the learners had to deduce the right step in
the diagnostic process from the subsequent solution
step in the example.
Instruments
Prior knowledge
The prior knowledge test measuring domain-speciﬁc
conceptual knowledge contained 21 MCQs, most of
which had been used in the German National Boards
medical examination. Two items were excluded from
analysis because of low item )total correlation. Thus
19 points could be achieved in this measure. The
reliability of the test was sufﬁcient (Cronbach /C213s
a = 0.63).
Diagnostic knowledge
The construct of diagnostic knowledge followed
considerations about relevant knowledge for
understanding domain-speciﬁc procedures. There-
fore, it comprised conceptual, strategic and teleo-
logical knowledge. The 19 conceptual knowledge
tasks of the prior knowledge test were presented
again after the learning phase (Cronbach /C213s
a = 0.60). In order to measure strategic knowledge,
10 key feature problems were applied.
28,29 A max-
imum of 29 points could be achieved. The reli-
ability score was 0.72 (Cronbach /C213s a). Additionally,
three problem-solving items, which functioned as
measures for strategic and teleological knowledge,
were used. In each item, the students had to answer
three questions. They had to generate their leading
diagnosis from the information given in a clinical
case scenario. Furthermore, they were asked to
explain their decision and to describe the under-
lying pathophysiological processes (maximum:
20 points; Cronbach /C213s a = 0.73).
The three tests operationalising diagnostic
knowledge correlated with Pearson coefﬁcients
of 0.45 )0.63. The reliability of the aggregated
diagnostic knowledge measure (maximum:
68 points) was 0.85 (Cronbach /C213s a).
Sustainability of the learning environment was
assessed by a regular MCQ examination which
consisted of 30 questions measuring primarily
conceptual knowledge in the domain of internal
medicine (maximum: 30 points; Cronbach /C213s
a = 0.68). Seven of these questions dealt with the
content matter of the learning environment
(arterial hypertension); the rest of the items
referred to other aspects of internal medicine.

Time-on-task
Time-on-task was recorded automatically by the
computer-based learning environment.
Procedure
After a short introduction, students completed the
MCQ test measuring prior knowledge, which was
followed by the learning session, in which the
students worked through the worked examples. After
a 15-min pause, the students worked on the diag-
nostic knowledge tests. Six weeks after the experi-
ment, the regular MCQ examination took place.
Statistical analyses
Effects of the two instructional measures on time-on-
task and sustainability effects were analysed by
variance analyses. In order to determine effects on
diagnostic knowledge, a general linear model (GLM)
was speciﬁed for each knowledge aspect. In the GLM,
the instructional measures were integrated as inde-
pendent variables and prior knowledge and time-
on-task as control variables. Partial g
2 was used as a
measure for effect strength. For bivariate
correlations, Pearson product )moment correlation
coefﬁcients were applied.

DISCUSSION
The primary objective of this study was to facilitate
students/C213diagnostic knowledge in a sustainable
manner. Therefore, a case-based, worked example
approach was realised in a computer-based learning
environment. In order to assure internal validity,
differences in time-on-task and prior knowledge were
statistically controlled for. Furthermore, the students
were randomly assigned to the four experimental
conditions.
The results show that the acquisition of diagnostic
knowledge is mainly fostered by providing erroneous
examples in combination with elaborated feedback.
When only KCR feedback is given, erroneous exam-
ples are detrimental. Against the background of the
rather short time-on-task invested by learners in all
conditions, the effects of the two instructional mea-
sures are remarkable. They conﬁrm pedagogical
considerations about the learning potential of
errors.
19 The unfavourable effect of erroneous
examples in combination with KCR feedback on
knowledge acquisition replicates ﬁndings of studies
in which erroneous examples were provided without
informative feedback measures.
20 In addition, these
ﬁndings are in line with current feedback research in
which the effectiveness of informative feedback
measures is stressed, at least in complex learning.
23
For most students, the information that a speciﬁc
diagnostic conclusion or procedure is not adequate
seems not to be sufﬁcient to induce deep conceptual
understanding. The information deﬁcit in the con-
ditions with KCR feedback, especially when learners
are confronted with erroneous examples, must be
compensated for by effective self-explanation.
7,8,11
However, as Renkl 10 showed, a lot of learners process
example information rather superﬁcially. As a result,
the full potential of the learning method is not
tapped. In fact, at least in the context of complex
learning environments, the feedback given must
inform students why the respective step in the
diagnostic process is wrong and which speciﬁc
conclusion or procedure is adequate. It is clear that
effective processing of this additional information is
not without cost: in our study, elaborated feedback
resulted in a substantial increase in learning time.
However, from a pedagogical perspective, this
additional investment in time-on-task pays off, at
least when erroneous examples are provided.
Six weeks after the experiment had concluded,
medium effects of the learning environment on
conceptual knowledge were still signiﬁcant. The fact
that this effect only occurred when the learners had
to answer MCQs focusing on content aspects repre-
sented in the learning environment validates the
sustainability effect. From a pedagogical perspective,
this ﬁnding is astonishing because the learning
sessions were short and the learning environment was
targeted at fostering not conceptual knowledge, but
diagnostic knowledge, which includes strategic and
teleological knowledge components.
OUTLOOK
If the positive ﬁndings of our study can be replicated,
this learning environment should be integrated into
the regular clinical curriculum at medical schools.
Concerning further studies, sustainability analyses
should include all aspects of diagnostic knowledge. In
addition, in order to gain more penetrating insights
into the sustainability of the instructional measures,
further analyses should include larger experimental
groups which enable differentiated comparisons. Fur-
thermore, thinking-aloud procedures
30 should be
employed in order to investigate effects of erroneous
examples and feedback on the quality of the learning
process. Only by recording the learners /C213self-explana-
tions can more direct indicators for pedagogically
desired processes of schema induction be won.

How we created virtual patient cases for
primary care-based learning
E. C. ADAMS 1, C. J. RODGERS 1, R. HARRINGTON 1, M. D. B. YOUNG 2 & V. K. SIEBER 3
1John Radcliffe Hospital, UK, 2University of Oxford, UK, 3University of Surrey, UK
Introduction
Virtual patient (VP) cases have been defined as ‘interactive
computer simulations of real-life clinical scenarios for the
purpose of medical training, education or assessment’ (Ellaway
et al. 2006). VP cases are particularly valuable for the
construction of clinical reasoning skills, which are notoriously
challenging to teach (Balla & Edwards 1986).
We present our preliminary experiences and early appli-
cation of a selection of video-enriched VP cases designed to
meet some of the specific pedagogical challenges of under-
graduate education in primary care. The VP cases give
students opportunities to practise and refine unique clinical
reasoning skills typically deployed by general practitioners
(GPs) (Balla & Edwards 1986).
Tailored VP cases have been created for a variety of
specialties ranging from geriatrics to paediatrics (Orton &
Mulhausen 2008; Gill et al. 2010). Clinical reasoning differs
between medical specialities; in particular, GPs draw on
unique strategies (Heneghan et al. 2009), which may not be
explicitly taught. VP cases can be used to multiply patient
encounters providing a bank of verbal and non-verbal
experiences (Cook & Triola 2009) which may accelerate
acquisition of targeted clinical reasoning skills. VP scenarios
are currently used in some areas of primary care education,
such as maintenance of certification examinations (American
Board of Family Medicine) (Sumner & Hagen 2008) and to
quantify variability in primary care physician decision making
(e.g. assessing qualified GPs in the treatment of depression in
standardised VPs) (Hooper et al. 2008).
Diagnostic strategies employed by GPs have recently been
defined (Heneghan et al. 2009), providing some clear learning
outcomes to instruct VP case design. Little is reported in the
literature about how GPs acquire their clinical reasoning skills,
but experience is likely to have an important role (Heneghan
et al. 2009). During the consultation, GPs generate prompt
diagnostic hypotheses (Elstein et al. 1972). Fast hypothesis
generation often depends on prior experience allowing ‘ spot
diagnosis’o r‘ pattern recognition ’. We chose to use real
patient videos as the basis of our VP cases to provide a virtual
‘prior experience’ to enable these strategies. Genuine patient
videos also offer experience in the interpretation of patient
narrative such as a ‘ classic history’ or patients ‘ self-reporting’o f
a diagnosis which GPs also draw on to make diagnoses
(Heneghan et al. 2009).
Video enrichment of VP cases has previously been shown
to be beneficial. One study found that users develop enhanced
cognitive and meta-cognitive processing when using video-
enriched cases compared to text alone (Balslev et al. 2010).
The advantages of using video cases to educate non-experts in
diagnostic strategies for paediatrics were recently highlighted;
patient video cases were found to ‘ strongly stimulate clinical
diagnostic reasoning processes ’ (Balslev et al. 2010).
GPs use further strategies such as ‘ restricted rule-outs ’ and
‘ probabilistic reasoning ’ to refine their initial diagnosis
(Heneghan et al. 2009). The strategy of ‘ restricted rule-outs ’
involves synthesising a short list of serious diagnoses which
must be excluded. Key questions then elicit symptoms
suggestive of these diagnoses ( red flags ). For ‘ probabilistic
reasoning’, clinicians estimate a pre-test probability of a
patient having a particular pathology and then adjust this
probability in the light of test results. Diagnostic decision tree
software can be used to create VP cases that give virtual
experience of these real-time clinical reasoning techniques.
Follow-up of and reflection on patients is a powerful
discipline for the learning and construction of clinical
reasoning skills (Kassirer 2010), but this is limited by short
Practice points
. The unique diagnostic approaches used by GPs tend not
to be explicitly taught to medical students.
. VP cases can be tailored using decision-making software
to give students experience of primary care specific
clinical reasoning skills.
. Collection, over time, of patient videos provides a
valuable resource for enrichment of VP cases and should
be encouraged.
. Our suggested ‘toolkit for success’ can be used as a
starting point for developing projects which use patient
videos.

student rotations. VP cases can be used to compress time,
allowing students to observe strategies such as ‘ test of time ’o r
‘ test of treatment ’ which GPs may use to define their diagnosis
(Heneghan et al. 2009). This compression of time also allows
the evolution of chronic disease, longitudinal management and
treatment effects to be illustrated.
On the basis of our preliminary experience and early
application of a series of VP cases, we outline our methods for
designing and utilising video enriched VP cases and describe
how we tailored the cases to promote the acquisition of
primary care specific clinical reasoning skills.
How we created the VP cases
VP case selection
We identified key core curriculum topics from the University of
Oxford’s undergraduate primary care syllabus and selected
dyspepsia, low back pain, dysuria and cardiovascular disease
for VP case development. In addition to their core nature,
these topics were also selected for their amenability for the
inclusion of the clinical reasoning strategies outlined above.
We do not see this as a comprehensive case list, but rather as a
series for pilot study, proof of concept and proof of value.
VP case design
Undergraduate primary care rotations are often short. This
means that students are unlikely to observe consultations or
meet patients suffering from all of the core curricular presen-
tations to primary care. The aim of our video enriched VP
cases is to simulate GP consultations revolving around these
core presentations, giving students the opportunity to be active
participants in the consultations in a virtual way. Table 1 shows
how the various primary care specific diagnostic strategies
have guided VP case design.
The VP cases are principally intended for self-directed
learning, but could also be used as a teaching tool in a small
group or lecture setting. On average, each VP case has
10 questions, comprised of a mixture of true/false questions
and multiple best answer questions. The VP cases are linear in
design meaning that all students will attempt all questions, but
there are optional extra activities e.g. considering a clip of a
patient describing their attempts to quit smoking in the
cardiovascular disease prevention case. Participants also
have the autonomy to repeat video clips or skip them
according to their preferences. The average time taken for a
student to complete a case is approximately 10 min.
An outline ( prototype) for each case was drawn up to
include essential content from the syllabus and key elements
to a consultation on this topic. Quandary (http://
www.halfbakedsoftware.com/) was chosen from among alter-
native systems for creating and delivering the decision-making
scenarios (e.g. Labyrinth – http://labyrinth.mvm.ed.ac.uk/ and
SBL Interactive – http://www.sblinteractive.org/) because of
its usability and the ease with which it could be customised to
create cases. Importantly, it allows a decision tree to be
constructed with multiple ways of reaching the same result,
with penalties applied for wrong answers.
VP video collection and edition
We utilised recordings from the patient video library of a GP
educator (RH) and also made new recordings to fill content
gaps, with the advantage that we could pre-plan questions to
elicit content-specific responses related to our prototype
decision trees. Valid consent was obtained from all patients
to use their video for educational purposes within the
university virtual learning environment.
Videos were edited (Apple iMovie) and compressed as
Flash video, to an appropriate bit rate for web delivery.
The appropriate size varies according to the web delivery
system used, but most clips were 1–3 MB with a maximum size
of 10 MB.
VP case review
Before VP case upload, a review process was undertaken; an
independent GP educator reviewed the cases for content
accuracy and appropriateness. A member of the university
learning technologies team reviewed the technological
aspects. Given that the VP cases were intended for
self-directed student learning, we asked four students to
individually attempt the cases to ensure usability before
uploading the cases to the virtual learning environment.
Feedback on the VPs
Feedback was collected on the accessibility, popularity and
any perceived disadvantages of each VP case. A free text box
(to allow open ended responses) formed the final page of each
case. In addition to qualitative feedback, quantitative data
were collected on the proportion of students reaching the
feedback page (meaning they finished the case) and the
number of attempts made at each case per student.
What’s next ... ?
In the light of our experiences, we highlight a number of
challenges and future directions for the development of
primary care VPs.
Content for VPs
We can speculate intuitively that certain topics, particularly
with distinctive visual cues or classic patient narratives, would
gain more value from patient video enrichment. Common
presenting complaints should be prioritised along with rarer
cases which are easily missed without prior experience. There
is an unanswered question relating to when video recording of
a consultation becomes inappropriate (e.g. recording acutely
unwell patients and sensitive topic areas such as sexual and
mental health issues), good guidance can be found at
http://www.cherri.mvm.ed.ac.uk/cherri.pdf
Quality and availability of patient videos is a limiting factor.
We want to encourage GPs to collect patient videos for
educational purposes. A bank of patient video clips built up
over time, associated with appropriate consent (see below),
could be an invaluable resource to enable similar projects.
