INTRODUCTION
The amount and complexity of information medical
students are asked to master are exponentially
increasing. One approach to help students overcome
this information overload is to identify strategies that
help students acquire knowledge more efﬁciently.
Cognitive load theory and knowledge organisation
concepts can help indesigning such learningstrategies.
Information overload through the lens of cognitive
load theory
Cognitive load theory views the challenges of learning
through the ﬁnite limitations of working memory.
1
Working memory can process only three to seven
information elements.
1 When a subject matter
involves multiple interacting elements, it can over-
whelm working memory and become difﬁcult to
learn. Traditionally, complex subjects with many
interacting elements are taught by presenting each
element separately to reduce cognitive load.
1,2 For
example, learning cardiac physical examination
requires students to master lists of ﬁndings for each
relevant diagnosis. However, when students face a
patient with an unknown systolic murmur, they must
integrate all of this information to arrive at a
diagnosis, a task that presents a tremendous chal-
lenge to working memory. An alternative approach is
to explicitly teach how the elements interact by
organising information into schemas
1 or representa-
tions of diagnoses distinguished by relevant clinical
and pathophysiologic variables. Schemas reduce
cognitive load by presenting the most important links
between interacting elements.
Schemas and knowledge organisation
Items of knowledge acquired by novices are often
stored in long-term memory as isolated facts. Isolated
facts are hard to recall and apply to clinical problems
because they are not linked to other relevant infor-
mation.
3 In order for this information to be useful in
solving clinical problems, it needs to be reorganised
around clinical ﬁndings and concepts. 2 This requires
trainees to link multiple causal hypotheses and
elaborate on them in order to build an understand-
ing of the underlying concept. Bordage describes this
highly linked conceptual knowledge as ‘compiled’.
3
Schemas group diagnoses by relevant clinical and
pathophysiologic variables. Therefore, the provision
of schemas is hypothesised to aid in the development
of compiled knowledge because schemas present the
information in a structured, clinically relevant way.
Schemas and clinical reasoning
Diagnostic reasoning strategies used by novice learn-
ers include hypothetico-deductive and schema-based
reasoning. Elstein et al.
4 describe hypothetico-
deductive reasoning as a process whereby clinicians
formulate and test hypotheses in a sequential fashion.
By contrast, schema-based reasoning is a process in
which key clinical features are used to include or
exclude sets of diagnoses. In an observational study,
Coderre et al.
5 found that novice medical students
achieved higher diagnostic success when employing a
schema-based strategy compared with a hypothetico-
deductive strategy. It is tempting to attribute the
higher diagnostic success to schema-based reasoning.
However, the use of schemas may also be a surrogate
for students with a more thorough understanding of
the clinical problem.
5
Relating knowledge organisation and reasoning
strategies
Knowledge organisation and reasoning strategies are
likely to be linked.
3,6 Dispersed knowledge acquired
through rote memorisation might force hypothetico-
deductive reasoning. Conversely, highly compiled
knowledge stored as elaborate causal networks may
promote schema-based reasoning. Therefore,
teaching schemas may have beneﬁcial effects in both
promoting more expert knowledge organisation and
facilitating expert-like reasoning.
Testing a schema-based approach
Previous studies of schema-based instruction
identiﬁed improved test scores and better diagnos-
tic accuracy when schemas were compared with
traditional lists or tables for teaching in nephro-
logy
7,8 and congenital cardiology. 9 These studies
suggest that schemas provide information in a
structure that enables the use of schema-based
reasoning. However, this evidence comes from non-
randomised retrospective comparisons in which
the effect of schemas may have been confounded
by differences among students in level of
expertise.
7–9
Seasoned clinicians have been critical of
schema-based instruction, arguing that schemas
cannot prepare students to reason through an
unlearned diagnosis.
8,9 Even experts abandon
schematic reasoning and adopt hypothesis testing
when faced with an unfamiliar problem.
10 Novice
students taught with a schema have not had to
navigate the material using a hypothetico-deductive

approach. As a result, students may struggle when
encountering untaught diagnoses.
Cardiac physical diagnosis provides a good model to
test the effect of schema-based instructional guidance
for several reasons. Firstly, multiple studies have
documented poor cardiac auscultatory skills among
senior medical students and residents, and resulting
low rates of diagnostic success (19–55%).
11–15
Secondly, traditional teaching of cardiac physical
diagnosis involves diagnosis-speciﬁc lists of features,
structured around steps in the cardiac physical
examination. This approach leads a novice learner to
hypothetico-deductive reasoning until repeated
encounters promote the development of individual
schemas. Thirdly, a high-ﬁdelity cardiopulmonary
simulator (CPS), Harvey
/C210 (Gorden Center for
Research in Medical Education, University of Miami,
Miami, FL, USA), which can mimic a wide range of
clinically relevant pathology for learning and test-
ing,
16 is available.
We aimed to test the effects of schema-based
instruction in comparison with those of a traditional
framework on the acquisition of cardiac auscultation
skills among novices in a randomised trial. We
hypothesised that schema-based instruction would
foster clinically relevant knowledge (hereafter
referred to as ‘structured knowledge’), increase
schema-based reasoning and improve diagnostic
accuracy. We also hypothesised that schema-based
instruction would increase diagnostic error compared
with traditional instruction for lesions that students
had not encountered before.
METHODS
Population
Year 2 medical students at the University of Toronto
were invited to participate. Students had previously
completed two 4-hour sessions covering the
components of the cardiac physical examination. All
participants provided informed consent.
Design
The study design featured case-based learning using
Harvey
/C210 , a CPS that reproduces visual, tactile and
auditory ﬁndings of the cardiac examination,
designed at the Gordon Center for Research in
Medical Education, University of Miami (Miami,
FL, USA). Participants attended a 15-minute
orientation.
Participants attended one of 14 sessions, each of
which included up to ﬁve participants. Sessions were
randomised into two categories to include a control
sample that received an instructional framework
based on the traditional approach (Fig. 1) and an
intervention sample that received an instructional
framework based on a diagnostic schema (Fig. 2).
Both frameworks contained the same information.
However, the organisation of the information
differed. The traditional framework (Fig. 1) was
structured around individual valvular lesions and
listed the 10 clinical features of each diagnosis in a
table format. The schema framework (Fig. 2)
grouped diagnoses according to clinical features
based on murmur location and timing (e.g. ‘apex
beat’, ‘radiation’ and ‘character’ for a murmur heard
at the apex).
Before the schemas were developed, we conducted a
search for existing frameworks in the literature. This
revealed two schemas that were inappropriate for the
study. One schema used a ﬁnding not available on
the simulator, hepatomegaly, as a key distinguishing
feature of cardiac lesions,
17 whereas the other was a
cumbersome, long framework beyond the scope of a
novice.18 Therefore, two experts with 10 years of
experience in cardiac physical examination were
consulted to develop an appropriate schema. The
schema was revised based on pilot data.
The study was divided into four phases: learning;
consolidation; testing, and retesting. The ﬁrst three
phases all occurred in the same session. Retesting
occurred 2–4 weeks later. All written materials were
handed to the facilitator at the end of the session to
prevent any contamination between groups.
Learning phase
In groups of two to ﬁve students, participants were
asked to deduce the diagnosis of four unknown
cardiac lesions (aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis,
mitral regurgitation and ventricular septal defect) on
the simulator using the assigned framework. A
facilitator was available for technical troubleshooting,
but did not participate in the learning process. Each
participant was asked to record his or her diagnosis
and the key features that had led to it. Once the
group had ﬁnished, participants were given a written
answer guide. The group was allowed 15 minutes to
resolve any incorrect diagnoses or clarify examination
features. This case-based, collaborative design was
intended to foster learning while limiting the effects
of instructional guidance to the framework provided.

Participants individually completed a written test

Retesting was limited to the written test by logistical

Written test
Participants completed a 19-question written test

factual knowledge questions. The written test was
marked by two researchers blinded to group alloca-

How do schemas beneﬁt novices? The hypothesis that
schemas beneﬁt novices by modifying knowledge
organisation and diagnostic reasoning strategies is
supported by our data. The results on the written test
provide evidence that schemas modiﬁed knowledge
organisation by increasing the amount of structured
knowledge without changing factual knowledge of
diagnoses. The magnitude of the effect (38–40%) is
similar to that in a previous study in which schemas
were found to improve scores on nephrology questions
by 30%.
8 Although reasoning strategy was not directly
measured (for fear of overwhelming novices with a
verbal protocol), schema-instructed students were
more likely to report features from the schema in
arriving at their diagnosis. This suggests a higher use of
schema-based reasoning by schema-instructed students.
Is there a downside to schema-based instruction? We
anticipated lower diagnostic accuracy on untaught
lesions among students instructed with schemas
because they may be less likely to generate non-
schema-based correct features. Although the tradi-
tional instruction group did generate a greater
number of correct features for untaught lesions, this
did not translate into higher diagnostic success. In
fact, the schema-based instruction group had 30%
higher diagnostic success. Two explanations are
possible. Firstly, the traditional instruction group
identiﬁed more incorrect features. Incorrect features
may have a derailing effect on diagnostic reasoning.
Secondly, the schema-based instruction group iden-
tiﬁed more schema-based features. Schema-based
features may be more helpful in the diagnostic
process than non-schema-based features as they help
distinguish diagnoses. Importantly, we cannot
generalise these ﬁndings to all diagnoses as we did
not assess diagnoses or feature combinations not
provided in the instructional material.
Our study has several limitations. Firstly, it was
conducted at a single centre. Our conclusions would
be strengthened by replication elsewhere. Secondly,
practical testing was immediate. With further time to
study and digest material, the beneﬁt of a schema
might be reduced. Thirdly, only novice learners
participated. It is unclear how our ﬁndings might

Abstract The study reported in this article concerns the questions what and how fourth-
year medical students can learn from a series of cases that have a similar underlying
problem. This question is crucial in the theoretical sense as it looks at mechanisms of
updating and improving knowledge structures, which are conjectured to consist of ‘illness
scripts’, which integrate knowledge about enabling conditions for a disease, the underlying
fault, and the consequences or signs and symptoms of the disease. It was found that much
learning was implicit, whilst students explicitly paid attention to variations in enabling
conditions and consequences, which led to improvement of these knowledge components.
Integration of biomedical knowledge into the fault component was, however, hampered by
lack of knowledge and by misconceptions that students were unable to debug in the
absence of learning resources or detailed feedback. The practical importance of this study

Learning medicine
One of the things you learn at a very young age is that certain conditions in your envi-
ronment or in your own behaviour can lead to pain and other discomfort. This knowledge is
learned from lessons of the format \do/don’t do this—or else—you’ll get ill[. Sometimes
these lessons are reinforced by the experience warned for, which in turn can then be
strengthened by the ﬁnal part of the lesson \I told you![. The following are examples of
such lessons: ‘‘Don’t eat raw meat, or else you’ll get food poisoning’’; ‘‘put on your coat,
or else you’ll catch a cold’’ and ‘‘wash your hands, or else you’ll catch the ﬂu.’’ In answer
to children’s ceaseless questions ‘Why?’ and ‘What is that?’, these lessons can soon
become rather complex. The ﬁrst author remembers that her aunt once forbade her to lick
the bowl clean in which this aunt had prepared cake dough, a treat otherwise, but now it
had been made with duck eggs, two large, greenish eggs with big, very yellow yolks. Her
question ‘Why?’ received the answer that it might give her typhoid fever, a disease—she
was told—that had almost killed her mother when she was a young girl.
Such lessons result in knowledge structures that link enabling conditions (entities,
events, situations that can threaten your health) to consequences (pain, fever, and worse),
and the behaviours needed for prevention or cure (take medicine, get a bandage, bed rest,
chicken soup, etc.). These elements are held together with stories about ‘How’ that can
happen, and that teach children about the faults, which are the underlying mechanisms of
genetic conditions, germs, defence, healing, etc. These knowledge structures can be seen as
the rudimentary forms of more generic scripts that develop with experience, with slots that
have default values and can be instantiated with the speciﬁc value of a certain case,
internally linked by a temporal and causal structure (Schank and Abelson 1977). The
scripts have been called ‘illness scripts’ by Feltovich and Barrows ( 1984). Illness scripts
consist of enabling conditions for a certain disease, the consequences of that disease, and
the biomedical fault that explains how the enabling conditions can lead to consequences.
Physicians’ clinical experience has resulted in very extended, detailed, and differentiated
illness scripts. The scripts are organised in memory based on their similarities and dif-
ferences, and on levels of abstraction and generality. Activated and instantiated illness
scripts generate a diagnosis if the case ﬁndings have acceptable slot values. Otherwise,
related scripts are activated or a temporary mental model is created, in which the fault
mechanism is provisionally adapted based on other knowledge and case ﬁndings (Feltovich
and Barrows 1984; Lesgold et al. 1988).
The study of medicine is very much the study of faults, especially in the ﬁrst years of
traditional curricula when the biomedical topics are taught. Later the clinical courses
follow that describe the appearance, epidemiology, pathophysiology, course, treatment,
and management of diseases. In practice, both kinds of knowledge are needed, which
requires that they be integrated. How important biomedical knowledge is in practice and
when this integration takes place have been much debated in the medical education lit-
erature. Many practitioners stated and still state that the medical curriculum was

overloaded with biomedical knowledge and that it was hardly used in practice (see, for
instance, Bordage 1987). Patel et al. (Patel et al. 1989) argued that biomedical knowledge
and clinical knowledge were two worlds apart. Clinical knowledge would be used in
clinical reasoning, whilst biomedical knowledge would be used in case explanation. Still
others (Schmidt and Boshuizen 1993) claimed that with higher levels of expertise bio-
medical knowledge and clinical knowledge would become integrated, and that biomedical
knowledge was used when needed, in diagnosis as well as in explanation. Reorganisation
of biomedical knowledge is needed to integrate it in the fault part of illness scripts.
Knowledge restructuring
Two important ﬁndings provided the grounds for the conclusion that higher levels of
expertise are associated with higher levels of integration (Schmidt and Boshuizen 1993):
First, novices and experts used hardly any biomedical knowledge in diagnosis and case
explanation, whilst intermediates did so to a large extent. However, comparison of the case
explanations by students and experts with a model explanation revealed that the percentage
of concepts that were identical increased sharply with higher expertise levels. Furthermore,
a content analysis of the experts’ explanation revealed that the concepts used were at an
intermediary level of detail, between basic biomedical knowledge and clinical concepts,
with a high explanatory power regarding the case ﬁndings. Examples are ‘sepsis’, ‘micro-
emboli’, and ‘aortic insufﬁciency’. Novices and intermediates on the other hand used very
detailed concepts, for instance explaining the speciﬁc temperature pattern included in the
expert concept ‘sepsis’. Second, students’ performance was largely affected by reducing
the case processing time in the experiment, whilst experienced physicians were hardly
inﬂuenced. Students needed the whole 3 min and 30 s to reason through the case step-by-
step activating their detail-level knowledge, and failed this completely when they were
given only 30 s. Experts were hardly affected.
Based on these ﬁndings and on what is known about the way medical students were
educated, Schmidt and Boshuizen (1993) theorised that initially students build networks of
thousands of concepts. Through repeated use in solving clinical cases, these networks
become validated and connected whilst links are strengthened, and the prominence of
certain concepts and groups of concepts changes. In this process, certain higher-level
concepts, which Schmidt and Boshuizen called ‘encapsulating’ concepts, such as the ones
given above, come to stand for the entire detailed networks of clinical and biomedical
concepts.
This assumption that knowledge restructuring is vital in medical expertise development
is further supported by the ﬁndings of Woods and colleagues (Woods 2007; Woods et al.
2005), who showed that this kind of integrated biomedical knowledge made clinical
knowledge more robust and improved clinical reasoning, whilst Rikers et al. ( 2005)
showed that experts’ biomedical knowledge is always co-activated with clinical knowledge
even in routine situations. Finally, researchers have found that problem-oriented knowl-
edge structures had a positive effect on diagnostic outcomes compared with knowledge
organisation according to generic principles (Coderre et al. 2009; Mclaughlin et al. 2010).
Together these studies suggest that continued and repeated experience with classes of
similar cases may result in the integration of biomedical knowledge in clinical knowledge
as fault knowledge in illness scripts, which in turn has a positive outcome on diagnostic
problem solving. Figure 1 demonstrates how biomedical knowledge and clinical knowl-
edge are linked in an illness script.

Implications for instruction and research question
In medical education, the development of such problem-oriented knowledge structures is
an important reason for teaching with clinical cases, as is done in problem-based curricula
(Boshuizen 2009). However, most curricula struggle with time available to cover so many
diseases and basic science topics that no time is spent on the study of sets of similar or
related cases to explore variations in the different elements of the illness scripts. Therefore,
the further development and differentiation of their illness scripts are left to the epide-
miological characteristics of the practices students will participate in later on in their
internships.
We consider the underlying assumption questionable that further illness script devel-
opment will take place automatically once students enter their internships. One reason is
that Prince et al. ( 2000) showed that, at least in the initial stages of learning in practice,
energy and attention go to very different practical aspects of practice. Furthermore, no
empirical data about the spontaneous learning processes when students meet multiple
cases with similar faults exist; hence, we do not have knowledge either about which
learning processes can be left to the students’ own devices and which processes may
beneﬁt from more focussed educational measures. The present study aims to ﬁll in blanks
regarding elements and processes of learning from multiple cases and its outcomes.
Therefore, we asked medical students who are about to enter their internships to reason
through a set of cases with the same underlying problem, gathering information about
their reasoning and knowledge development with think-aloud protocols, case explanations,
and learner reports.

Method
Participants
Thirty-one 4th-year undergraduate medical students of a medical school with a problem-
based learning (PBL) curriculum participated. Data were collected at the end of the academic
year, which means that the students had almost completed the preclinical part of the cur-
riculum and were about to enter their internships. In medical school, the students had worked
with clinical cases in different settings: paper cases in PBL sessions, simulated patients in the
skills lab, and early experience with real patients in the community and in hospitals. The
participants were randomly assigned to two groups who received different sets of endocri-
nological problems. All students repeatedly studied the basic mechanisms and clinical
consequences of the endocrinological problems in prior training. Due to no shows and
incomplete data sets, one group consisted of 14 students and the other of 17 students.
Materials
We developed two series of ﬁve cases with the same underlying pathophysiological pro-
cess but with different presentations and causes. One series consisted of polycystic ovaries
(PCO) cases and the other series of hyperprolactinaemia (HPA) cases. The core of both
disorders is an endocrine dysfunction in women leading to menstrual and fertility prob-
lems. A study by Dawson-Saunders et al. ( 1990) with expert clinical and biomedical
teachers had earlier indicated that endocrine feedback systems are very important (top 3 of
27) but not difﬁcult (easiest 3 of 27). A practice case and three ﬁller cases concerning other
menstrual problems were developed as well. All cases were based on real patients and
written in cooperation with a gynaecologist and an endocrinologist. The cases were
comparable in length and presented in a standard medical order successively describing
history taking, physical examination, lab ﬁndings, and additional examinations.
Procedure
The students were told that they would be presented with a series of cases and that their task
was to diagnose and explain each case and to learn as much as they could from all these cases.
No suggestions were given as to how the students could approach their learning tasks. Cases
were presented on a computer screen, and were segmented into meaningful sections con-
sisting of a couple of sentences that represented standard units of history taking, physical
examination, lab ﬁndings, and additional examinations. A mouse click brought on the next
unit. Students processed the cases whilst thinking aloud. The instruction was to express
everything that came up in their mind whilst going through a case. Consecutively, the par-
ticipants gave their diagnoses by typing them directly into a window in the presentation
programme and provided a pathophysiological explanation on paper. This format was chosen
to enable the use of graphical representations and reﬂection during explanation. After the
students had completed a case, the ofﬁcial diagnosis was given, as they would have received
similar feedback if they had encountered the patient as clerks in the hospital.
After the instructions, a practice case was used to make the students comfortable with
the procedure. The three ﬁller cases were interspersed as numbers 3, 5, and 7 to ensure
attentive case processing.

Finally, after all cases had been processed, the students were reminded of their task to
learn from the cases and to tell what they knew now about PCO or HPA (learner reports).
The students were probed with the concepts that are neutral to illness script categories,
generally used as headers in medical textbooks, and well known to the students: Deﬁnition,
epidemiology, pathophysiology, symptoms, physical examination, further examination,
differential diagnosis, and therapy. Thinking-aloud, explanation, and the learner reports
were audio-recorded and transcribed for further analysis.
Analysis
Progress of knowledge use
The progress of knowledge use over the cases up to the learner reports was charted by
identifying speciﬁc concepts in the protocols. These concepts were based on a list of
relevant encapsulating concepts for the case series, which together explain the fault in the
cases (see Appendix 1). Similar to the examples given above, these concepts differ in depth
and explanatory power. Two concepts in both series are directly linked to observable
consequences; those concepts are termed superﬁcial here. Another two concepts in both
series are also directly linked to consequences but are less observable. They are termed
intermediate here. The rest of the lists consist of concepts describing biomedical processes
and principles that are indirectly linked to enabling conditions and consequences. They are
described as deep (biomedical) concepts. The PCO cases are explained by nine deep
concepts, the HPA cases by ten. These lists were developed in cooperation with four
domain experts. Furthermore, development of misconceptions, reminders of earlier cases,
and language use (professional versus everyday language) were investigated.
Elaborate reasoning about the cases was seen during case processing (14 participants)
and afterward during the pathophysiological explanation (12 participants), whilst 4 of them
did so in both tasks. Therefore, these documents were analysed in combination. Outcomes
were compared with the learner reports.
Learning from the cases
The analysis of the learning process as expressed in the think-aloud protocols, the path-
ophysiological explanations, and the learner reports were developed in an iterative way.
Coding categories and scoring criteria were developed by going through a subset of cases
repeatedly until no changes were needed between cycles. The coding categories regarded
the phase in the learning process where most thinking took place (thinking aloud,
explaining the case, or in the learner report), occurrence of reminders of earlier cases,
biomedical reasoning, improvement over cases, remediation of misconceptions over cases
as well as in the learning reports, and language use. Interrater agreement over another
subset of 10 % revealed an average agreement of 73 %.
Content analysis of the learner reports
The third analysis regarded the results of knowledge development as expressed in the
learner reports. We took a model text description of that disorder, derived from medical
textbooks and checked by two domain experts as a basis for comparison. The model text
was segmented into meaningful wholes and classiﬁed into the same categories of clinical

texts that were used as probes. The segments were complex statements consisting of
several propositions. An example is ‘affected are females in the fertile stage of life’. The
numbers of segments per category were identical in the two cases. The following cate-
gories were added, as the learner reports happened to include statements that did not ﬁt the
standard categories: normal physiology (generic knowledge), inferences, and elaborations.
Utterances were mapped on these segments and coded as complete or partial ﬁts. Utter-
ances were classiﬁed as inferences when they could be described as conclusions students
drew within the relevant knowledge domain; they were classiﬁed as elaborations when
they were additions based on other related knowledge ﬁelds. Furthermore, the number of
metacognitive statements referring to knowledge monitoring processes (e.g., ‘I don’t know
if …’) were counted. Inferences, elaborations, and reasoning based on normal physiology
were categorised separately and taken as indicators for active knowledge construction and
reconstruction. Deﬁnition had three segments, epidemiology two, pathophysiology 21,
symptoms 14, physical examination six, further examination ﬁve, differential diagnosis
three, and therapy had seven segments. Scores in the pathophysiology category represent
the use of problem-oriented knowledge, the faults in illness scripts. Epidemiology repre-
sents the illness script category enabling conditions; symptoms and (additional) physical
examination regard consequences. Two independent raters coded the ﬁrst 10 learner
reports. The raters compared and discussed differences until they came to a full agreement.
The remaining learner reports were coded by one rater. Quantitative learner report mea-
sures were analysed with a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) with repeated
measures.
Results
Progress of knowledge use
Most students used more explicit, detailed reasoning in the ﬁrst case than in later cases in
the series. This pattern was more pronounced in the PCO group. Many students diligently
activated and sometimes painfully reconstructed their knowledge (e.g., participant 436, see
Table A in Online Appendix) when dealing with the ﬁrst case.
Use of speciﬁc fault concepts
The analyses of speciﬁc fault concepts (see Appendix 1) that were used in diagnosing and
explaining the cases and in the learner reports revealed that relatively most of the fault
concepts the students used were superﬁcial, followed by the intermediate concepts, and
then followed by the deep concepts (Table 1). Three values stood out in this pattern: the
relatively high number and proportion of deep concepts in the HPA protocols, the overall
small proportion of intermediate concepts in the HPA learner reports, and the high pro-
portion of intermediate concepts in the PCO protocols. No general trend was discernable in
the emergence or disappearance of deep concepts. In the intermediate concepts we saw,
however, that the concept of ‘endometrial proliferation’, which was most prominent in the
ﬁrst case presented, was followed by ‘anovulation’ in the later cases of the series, indi-
cating that the students extended their case representation over multiple cases. The most
explicit examples are participants 415, 416, and 428 (see Table C in Online Appendix).

Learning from the cases
Of the 31 participants, only 15 demonstrated in their dealings with the cases that they
learned from solving the cases. These participants became less uncertain, used more
speciﬁc language, gradually came to focus on the essential aspects of the biomedical
process, or showed more complete pathophysiological explanations (see Tables B and D
in Online Appendix). The following examples illustrate what students learned. One student
evaluated his prior knowledge in light of the cases dealt with: ‘‘It concerns a certain
hormonal disorder, in which I thought to have learned from literature that LH is always
high, oestrogen high and FSH low … but the cases show that it is sometimes different’’
(participant 422). Another concluded in the learner report that she had learned something
new: ‘‘I did not know it were so many [follicles]’’ (p 413). The other 16 students may have
learned but did not show this in their approach to the case, or in their learning reports.
Learning from multiple cases can be assumed to be most effective when students have
well-developed validated knowledge. The think-aloud protocols, explanations, and learner
reports showed that the knowledge of the majority of the participants in this study did not
really meet this criterion (Table 2 and see Tables A and C in Online Appendix). No
participant had all of the relevant knowledge available; 7 had very poor prior knowledge.
The other 24 had basic relevant knowledge that was, however, incomplete and error-prone.
Fourteen engaged in active biomedical reasoning aimed at improving errors or uncer-
tainties the students had recognised. This active debugging in the HPA series was mostly
done within a single case; in the PCO series, active debugging was extended over cases.
Six participants appeared able to—partially—remediate the misconceptions they had
expressed, whereas 2 participants chose to further ignore the errors they noticed. The
remaining 14 participants were either not aware that they made errors of reasoning or were
incapable of solving them, as the participants made errors persistently throughout the case
series. The most common and persistent misconception was that excessive amounts of
oestrogens are converted into androgens in fat cells leading to an androgenic appearance in
affected females, whilst it happens to be the other way round.

Discussion
This study departed from the observation that research and theory on illness script con-
struction by medical students emphasises the importance of the integration of—separately
taught—biomedical fault knowledge. This process requires restructuring of biomedical
knowledge, which is assumed to take place as a function of the application of such
knowledge on clinical problems. Within the limits of preclinical education, these processes
are supervised, for instance, in tutorial groups in PBL, but in clinical teaching settings,
teachers focus different things, e.g., differential diagnosis and treatment, whilst the stu-
dents’ main task is to take patients’ full history and examination and report that in the
patients’ records. Whilst in preclinical settings, the curriculum and teachers deﬁne which
cases are presented; in the clinical settings, it is the epidemiology of the time of the year
and speciﬁc hospital or outpatient clinic. Furthermore, feedback on the results is often
delayed, if indeed the doctor or student ever receives that feedback. This makes the clinic a
reduced learning setting. In this context, we situated our concern about what medical
students learn spontaneously from reasoning through a series of cases that have a similar
underlying biomedical problem and where only reduced feedback is provided. More
speciﬁcally, we wanted to know how knowledge about the constituent parts of illness
scripts (enabling conditions, fault, and consequences) develop, where we left the possi-
bility open that different parts do not develop in the same way.
The results can be summarised as follows:
(1) Students did learn from processing multiple cases even when the feedback is
restricted to the diagnosis. They built up representations faster, became more secure,

used more speciﬁc language, and tested their knowledge against case information.
Yet half of the students did not show this kind of learning.
(2) Most students learned from the variations in enabling conditions and consequences
components of the cases. Some students compared prior knowledge with case
ﬁndings, some actively compared cases, drawing conclusions about enabling
conditions and consequences, whilst others seemed to learn implicitly. No student
made errors in their conclusions.
(3) Learning from a series of cases appeared to have less positive outcomes regarding the
fault component of illness scripts. Many students had poor knowledge, including
misconceptions. Some tried, and one even succeeded in debugging these miscon-
ceptions, but the results of these enterprises never made it to the learner reports. Since
one of the probes for the learner report invited students to report on what they knew
now about the pathophysiology of the disease, this ﬁnding seems to indicate that the
students’ knowledge did not really improve. Other indicators for this lack of learning
or improving problem-oriented knowledge were (a) relative lack of use of deep
encapsulating concepts especially regarding endocrine regulation and (b) application
of generic biomedical knowledge and the emergence of elaborations and inferences in
the learner reports. These ﬁndings suggest that knowledge construction and
reconstruction were still in progress and were hampered by a lack of knowledge
and by deep misconceptions.
In summary, we may conclude that there is much implicit learning, which may lead to
faster recognition, strengthening of the links between concepts, and tuning of knowledge to
practical conditions (Anderson 1982). As many students did not show any explicit learning
processes, this result raises doubts about the students’ ability to take full advantage of
learning from cases. Furthermore, explicit learning anchored by given case ﬁndings con-
sisted of two types: comparison of case ﬁndings with prior knowledge and explicit com-
parison of cases. Both processes had positive outcomes, but in the current setting, this
learning is very dependent on whether the students’ attention is also drawn to co- and
invariation between cases (Marton and Pang 2006). Finally, explicit case explanations
based on deep concepts resulted in knowledge construction and debugging processes that
are considered to be conducive to knowledge network validation and (re)structuring, but
students were unable to complete these processes unsupported. We may conclude from
these analyses that students may learn patterns of and variations in enabling conditions and
consequences from this kind of learning situation but that unsupported case analyses are in
no way sufﬁcient for integrating biomedical knowledge in illness scripts.
Before answering the question which learning processes can be left to their own devices
and what the implications for teaching are, we must mention that the teaching hospital,
despite the term, is primarily a workplace where patients come ﬁrst, and where medical
students work and learn. Yet in this environment, patients are the ﬁrst learning resources,
apart from the medical and nursing staff and reference materials such as books and
databases (Dornan et al. 2008). In this context, we tend to conclude that students are well
able to learn the patterns and variations of enabling conditions and consequences inde-
pendently. However, learning can become more fruitful if students are supported to build a
case-base they can reﬂect on in a systematic way. Modern technology such as personal
digital assistants become rapidly integrated in student learning in the clinic (Garrett and
Jackson 2006; Ranson et al. 2007; Tempelhof 2009) as a resource or as an access point to
the students’ portfolio where they can upload case information and reﬂections. Buckley
et al. (2009) concluded in their review study that the higher-quality studies found suggested

123

that learning portfolios help medical students improve the integration of theory with
practice, and lead to greater self-awareness and reﬂection. Integration with the hospital
information and communication technologies-systems might be very worthwhile for
learning but is hindered by system safety measures and by patient privacy considerations.
The present results do not tell whether students will use resource information to debug a
misconception in biomedical knowledge, which is a required condition for integration. As
one—both teacher and student—is aware of poor knowledge and misconceptions only
during problem-solving, and since debugging is an effortful enterprise, it is doubtful
whether opportunities for impromptu case-based teaching events in the clinical practice
(e.g., in outpatient clinics, or grand rounds) are sufﬁcient. On top of that, active knowledge
debugging and integration should also take place off-line, outside the situation where the
problem was detected. Kassirer ( 2010) suggested a potentially powerful case conference
method, in which a maximum of 30 students, clerks, or interns participate. Participants
bring in their own cases. This is where the method might integrate with portfolio work. A
coach who is unfamiliar with the cases best supports the group in case analysis. The main
goal of these conferences is optimising clinical reasoning, but an important rule in the
reasoning process is ‘‘Working diagnoses, that is, hypotheses used for prognostic or
therapeutic recommendations, are evoked only after they are assessed for their adequacy in
explaining all positive, negative, and normal clinical ﬁndings, and for their pathophysio-
logic reliability—namely, a check on the reasonableness of causal linkages between
clinical events’’ (Kassirer 2010, p. 1119). The role of the coach is that all participants are
active and to prevent cognitive errors from being made. Though Kassirer himself focused
on clinical reasoning skill, cognitive restructuring should be a by-product of the process.
The focus of this study was theory development, that is, to ﬁnd out what students can
learn spontaneously from multiple cases. The outcomes were to a large extent inﬂuenced
by the speciﬁc case mixes. If medical educators were right that the topics at hand were
important and relatively easy, it is hard to say what will happen with more difﬁcult topics.
The instructional conclusions based on these outcomes regarded the clinical period in
which further learning should take place. Findings at the point of transition from one
learning environment to the next, or from theory to practice, always generate the question
whether education in the previous period should not have provided for this problem. Apart
from a policy issue, this issue also concerns pedagogical content knowledge. Prevention of
misconceptions is not a big issue in medical education literature. Feltovich et al. ( 1997)
warned against simpliﬁcation in such complex domains and instead advised multiple
perspectives and metaphors to make students appreciate the full complexity of the bio-
medical domain.
The strength of the present study is that it investigated unsupported, spontaneous
learning, which allowed us to draw conclusions about the learning processes and outcomes.
Some of these conclusions were based on what was present in the protocols; others were
based on what was not present. Though the latter conclusions play a small role in the
implications formulated, especially conclusions about implicit learning and not learning
should be further investigated with other methods.

Effect of enhanced analytic reasoning on

Abstract
Background: Diagnostic error can be caused by several types of cognitive bias, which may be reversed by enhancing analytic
reasoning.
Aims: To evaluate whether enhancing analytic reasoning can increase diagnostic accuracy in objective structured clinical
examination (OSCE) in medical students.
Methods: All fourth-year medical students, randomly assigned to the analytic reasoning or control groups, undertook the OSCE
with four cases using standardized patients. The analytic reasoning group was requested to list differential diagnoses and findings
compatible or not compatible with each diagnosis prior to providing a diagnosis, while the control group provided a diagnosis
without these processes. Mean diagnostic accuracy scores ( perfect score, 4.0) from four cases of OSCE were compared between
the two groups.
Results: One hundred forty-five students were randomly assigned to the analytic reasoning group ( n ¼ 65) or the control group
(n ¼ 80). The baseline characteristics, including grade point average and the scores from each patient encounter, were comparable
between groups. Mean diagnostic accuracy scores were significantly higher in the analytic reasoning group than in the control
group (3.40 /C6 0.66 versus 3.05 /C6 0.98; p ¼ 0.011).
Conclusion: Enhancement of analytic reasoning may improve diagnostic accuracy in novice doctors.
Introduction
Diagnostic errors comprise a large proportion of preventable
medical errors and can be a result of numerous types of
cognitive bias (Graber et al. 2005). Common cognitive bias
include premature closure (‘‘the tendency to stop considering
other possibilities after reaching a diagnosis’’), anchoring (‘‘the
tendency to perceptually lock onto salient features too early in
the diagnostic process’’), and confirmation bias (‘‘the tendency
to seek data to confirm, not refute, the hypothesis’’) (Croskerry
2003).
Analytic reasoning, one method used to combat bias, is a
reflective approach that involves the consideration of alterna-
tive diagnoses and of evidence to refute a diagnosis as well as
to support it (Norman & Eva 2010). However, there are few
studies evaluating the effect of analytic reasoning on reducing
diagnostic error (Mamede et al. 2010a, b). We conducted a
randomized controlled study to determine whether the
enhancement of analytic reasoning increases medical students’
diagnostic accuracy on the objective structured clinical exam-
ination (OSCE) using standardized patients.
Methods
This randomized control study was conducted in 2011 at Seoul
National University College of Medicine (Seoul, South Korea).
All fourth-year medical students participated in the OSCE ,
which consists of four cases (IgA nephropathy, neurogenic
diabetes insipidus, acute pyelonephritis, and exercise-induced
asthma) developed by the Seoul Kyeonggi CPX Consortium; it
was administered to nine examination groups of students over
3 days. Each case required 16 min to administer, with 1 min to
introduce the next case, 10 min for the student–standardized
patient encounter, and 5 min after the encounter for the
student to report the most probable diagnosis (Park et al.
2007).
The students were randomly assigned to nine examination
groups through a computerized random selection process.
Each examination group was also randomly assigned to either
the analytic reasoning group or the control group. After
encountering patients, students in the analytic reasoning group
received an answer sheet containing a table designed to
enhance analytic reasoning. Students in the analytic reasoning
group were asked to complete the table with differential
diagnoses and symptoms or signs compatible with or differing
from each diagnosis, and then provide one most probable
diagnosis. Students in the control group were simply asked to
provide one most probable diagnosis on an answer sheet that
lacked the table provided to the test group. Each group was
given 5 min to complete their respective answer sheets;
students in the reflective reasoning group had to complete
the table and provide a diagnosis within 5 min. Before and

The mean diagnostic accuracy scores ( perfect score, 4.0)

linear regression model in which age, sex, grade point

Student’s t-test was used to compare age, grade point average,

Results
A total of 145 fourth-year students were randomly assigned to
the analytic reasoning group ( n ¼ 65) or the control group
(n ¼ 80). Baseline characteristics, including grade point aver-
age, were comparable between groups (Table 1). OSCE scores
from encounters with standardized patients did not differ
significantly between the two groups.
Mean diagnostic accuracy scores were significantly higher
in the analytic reasoning group than in the control group
(3.40 /C6 0.66 versus 3.05 /C6 0.98; 95% CI of difference, 0.08–
0.62; p ¼ 0.016). In the analytic reasoning group, diagnostic
accuracy did not change significantly with respect to case
order ( p ¼ 0.93 for trend).
Discussion
While most previous studies evaluating the effect of analytic
reasoning on diagnostic accuracy used written examinations
(Mamede et al. 2008, 2010b), this study employed the OSCE
using standardized patients, which may better reflect real-life
clinical situations (Barrows 1993). In addition, this study did
not compel any experimental, artificial condition prohibiting
analytic reasoning to the control group. Instead, we evaluated
the value of enhancing analytic reasoning compared with
routine, usual reasoning in medical students.
The finding that scores from the patient encounters were
comparable between the two groups implies that students in
both groups obtained similar clinical information from the
standardized patients. Nonetheless, diagnostic accuracy was
significantly higher in the analytic reasoning group than in the
control group, suggesting that using an apparatus (in this case,
the table) to enhance analytic reasoning can help reduce
diagnostic error in clinical reasoning. Completing the table
presented on the answer sheet forced the consideration of
alternative diagnoses and of findings that conflicted with a
suspected diagnosis. These methods, in combination with the
analysis of compatible findings, might contribute to reducing
cognitive bias. These findings suggest that the training and
practice of analytic reasoning should be emphasized to
medical students and novice doctors.
This study has a few limitations. First, this study was
performed among fourth-year medical students just before
attaining the license of medical doctor. Therefore, these results
may not be generalizable to experienced doctors. However,
senior residents may be more susceptible to cognitive error
(e.g., availability bias) than junior residents, which can be
corrected with analytic reasoning (Mamede et al. 2010b).
Second, the effect of analytic reasoning on diagnostic accuracy
can be case specific. In this study, diagnostic accuracy
regarding the case of acute pyelonephritis was similar between
the groups. Because the clinical presentation of this case was
typical, students who took a heuristic ( pattern recognition)
approach may not have made diagnostic errors. Another study
has demonstrated contradictory results, suggesting that ana-
lytic reasoning exercised by medical students was ineffective
in complex cases, but effective in simple cases (Mamede et al.
2010a). That study’s findings suggest that analytic reasoning
may not be helpful if a case is too complex with respect to the
level of students’ medical knowledge.
In conclusion, this randomized controlled study demon-
strated that, among fourth-year medical students diagnosing
standardized patients, the enhancement of analytic reasoning

cases: the role of biomedical knowledge

OBJECTIVE General guidelines for teaching
clinical reasoning have received much atten-
tion, despite a paucity of instructional
approaches with demonstrated effectiveness.
As suggested in a recent experimental study,
self-explanation while solving clinical cases
may be an effective strategy to foster reason-
ing in clinical clerks dealing with less familiar
cases. However, the mechanisms that mediate
this beneﬁt have not been speciﬁcally investi-
gated. The aim of this study was to explore
the types of knowledge used by students when
solving familiar and less familiar clinical cases
with self-explanation.
METHODS In a previous study, 36 third-year
medical students diagnosed familiar and less
familiar clinical cases either by engaging in
self-explanation or not. Based on an analysis
of previously collected data, the present study
compared the content of self-explanation pro-
tocols generated by seven randomly selected
students while solving four familiar and four
less familiar cases. In total, 56 verbal protocols
(28 familiar and 28 less familiar) were seg-
mented and coded using the following catego-
ries: paraphrases, biomedical inferences,
clinical inferences, monitoring statements and
errors.
RESULTS Students provided more self-expla-
nation segments from less familiar cases
(M = 275.29) than from familiar cases
(M = 248.71, p = 0.046). They provided signiﬁ-
cantly more paraphrases (p = 0.001) and made
more errors (p = 0.008). A signiﬁcant interac-
tion was found between familiarity and the
type of inferences (biomedical versus clinical,
p = 0.016). When self-explaining less familiar
cases, students provided signiﬁcantly more
biomedical inferences than familiar cases.
CONCLUSIONS Lack of familiarity with a case
seems to stimulate medical students to engage
in more extensive thinking during self-explana-
tion. Less familiar cases seem to activate stu-
dents’ biomedical knowledge, which in turn
helps them to create new links between bio-
medical and clinical knowledge, and eventually
construct a more coherent mental representa-
tion of diseases. This may clarify the previously
found positive effect that self-explanation has
on the diagnosis of unfamiliar cases.

INTRODUCTION
Accurate clinical reasoning, a highly valued doctor’s
attribute, develops through years of practice. Knowl-
edge derived from research on medical expertise
has led to many suggestions on how to support the
development of students’ clinical reasoning skills.
1–3
For instance, teaching approaches should emphasise
acquiring domain-speciﬁc knowledge over general
problem-solving strategies, and also support the
integration of biomedical with clinical knowledge.
Teaching around examples, providing students with
many opportunities to engage in problem solving,
to reﬂect and elaborate on patients’ problems, are
approaches that have also been highlighted.
1–3 How-
ever, despite broad acceptance of these principles,
instructional approaches to help teachers apply
them are scarce, and their effectiveness remains to
be determined.
4–6
An effective strategy to foster the development of
clinical reasoning in clinical clerks is self-explana-
tion.
7 Generating self-explanations while diagnosing
a set of clinical cases, even without receiving feed-
back, resulted in better diagnostic performance
compared with students who did not self-explain.
However, this positive effect was only demonstrated
with unfamiliar clinical cases. Similarly, it has been
observed that the beneﬁt of self-explanation
increases when the problem at hand is complex,
and its effect seems more apparent on far transfer
tasks.
8,9 As an extension of the study by Chamber-
land and colleagues, 7 the present study explored
the types of knowledge used by students when self-
explaining familiar and less familiar clinical cases
and, in particular, the role of biomedical knowl-
edge.
Self-explanation is a constructive learning strategy
that consists of generating explanations to oneself
in response to learning material.
8,10 Consequently,
learners deepen their understanding of the material
and make their knowledge more meaningful, while
monitoring their evolving understanding. Self-expla-
nations are not necessarily formal and complete,
but may be fragmented, incorrect or incomplete;
reﬂecting, in fact, what the learner does and does
not understand.
8
It has been proposed that the activation of several
cognitive processes when self-explaining is responsi-
ble for learners’ improved understanding of the
learning material.
8 That is, while self-explaining
learners engage in knowledge elaboration and infer-
ence generation (i.e. drawing conclusions that go
beyond what the text explicitly states). This may
enable them to integrate new knowledge with prior
knowledge and to create links between pieces of
information within the material. It has also been
proposed that self-explanation triggers monitoring
processes.
8 While trying explicitly and actively to
make sense of the material, learners become more
aware of what they know or understand well, but
are also confronted with uncertainties, forgotten
information or with the limits of their prior knowl-
edge. Indeed, even incorrect or erroneous self-
explanations may promote learning if the learner,
detecting these misunderstandings, then tries to
resolve them.
8 Moreover, as a result of knowledge
elaboration and monitoring, knowledge restructur-
ing takes place, allowing the learner to build a more
coherent and integrated representation that facili-
tates transfer of learning.
8
For the acquisition of clinical reasoning skills, self-
explanation could be a useful knowledge-building
strategy, as most theories about developing medical
expertise are centred on the restructuring of medi-
cal knowledge.
3,11,12 According to the illness script
theory, medical students go through learning stages,
structuring knowledge differently at each stage, to
be kept in memory and used to solve clinical prob-
lems. That is, knowledge is ﬁrst organised into
complex causal networks that provide pathophys-
iological explanations for the causes and conse-
quences of disease.
3 Later, with exposure to clinical
problems and repeated application of biomedical
knowledge, the latter becomes encapsulated.
Further clinical experience then leads to the emer-
gence of illness scripts, which make scant use of
causal mechanisms, but are rich in the risk factors,
symptoms and signs that characterise real-life
clinical situations.
3
The transition from the preclinical to clinical educa-
tion (i.e. clerkship) has been associated with this
shift from biomedical to clinical knowledge.
13 That
is, less advanced students mainly use biomedical
knowledge to understand a case, whereas more
experienced ones understand it in clinical terms.
Biomedical knowledge used by students to solve
clinical problems is not necessarily very sophisti-
cated, but as long as it provides clear, plausible and
stable links between clinical features, it helps stu-
dents to create a coherent representation of a
case.
14 Biomedical knowledge is usually phrased by
students in terms of entities (e.g. bacteria, stone,
carcinoma) or in terms of organs, organ systems,

physiological functions (e.g. digestion) or basic
mechanisms (e.g. obstruction of the biliary tract).
By contrast, clinical knowledge refers to attributes
of people and their diseases, to the different ways a
disease can manifest itself in the patient (i.e. signs
and symptoms) and to relevant laboratory investiga-
tion and therapy.
13 Studies looking at the beneﬁts
of biomedical knowledge in the process of learning
clinical reasoning in novice diagnosticians suggest
that it may help students to construct more coher-
ent mental representations of diseases, increasing
retention in the longer term and helping them to
diagnose difﬁcult cases.
15,16
Our previous study with medical students in clerk-
ship showed that self-explanation while diagnosing
cases, compared with no self-explanation,
improved diagnostic performance on new cases
1 week later. However, this beneﬁcial inﬂuence
was only present for less familiar cases.
7 Could
self-explanation for less familiar cases support the
development of a more coherent representation?
To what extent could biomedical knowledge play
a role in learning clinical reasoning through self-
explanation in medical students? Students’ verbal
protocols generated during self-explanation repre-
sent a window into the cognitive processes in
which they engage while learning.
17,18 The content
analysis of self-explanations generated by medical
students while solving clinical cases could there-
fore provide insight into the mechanisms that
mediate the self-explanation effect on diagnostic
performance.
7
The present study attempted to better understand
why self-explanation is beneﬁcial with less familiar
cases. It aimed to explore the types of knowledge
students use when self-explaining by conducting a
content analysis of protocols generated by students
while solving familiar and less familiar cases. It was
hypothesised that when reasoning on less familiar
cases, students would generate more self-explana-
tions and reactivate more biomedical knowledge
than when solving familiar cases.
METHODS
Participants
Thirty-six third-year medical students from the
University of Sherbrooke, Sherbrooke, Quebec,
Canada participated in the initial study. 7 They had
to diagnose 12 randomly presented clinical cases
(four familiar, four less familiar and four ﬁller
cases) with or without self-explanations. Recordings
of self-explanations were available from 14 of the
18 students involved in the self-explanation group.
Each record comprised of self-explanations while
solving four familiar clinical cases and four less
familiar cases. For the secondary analysis reported
here, a sample of seven students (50%) was ran-
domly selected from the 14 available students. We
did not analyse the data of all 14 students because
of the elaborateness analysing these types of proto-
col. Accordingly, 56 protocols were transcribed
and analysed, 28 about familiar cases and 28 about
less familiar cases.
Materials
Eight clinical cases concerning two different clinical
topics, one familiar topic and one less familiar
topic, were used in this study. The level of familiar-
ity was established a priori for the whole group of 36
students and derived from students’ prior exposure
to similar clinical problems in the undergraduate
problem-based learning curriculum. Heart failure
was identiﬁed as a familiar topic and jaundice as a
less familiar topic. Four different cases for each of
these two clinical topics were developed by experi-
enced doctors. Thus, as in the initial study, familiar
cases refer to heart failure cases and less familiar
cases refer to jaundice cases. Case summaries,
approximately 300 words, included the chief com-
plaint, patient’s background, medical history, physi-
cal examination and the results of laboratory tests.

Procedure
In the initial study,
7 participants were tested indi-
vidually. The instructions to the students were as
follows. Self-explaining was deﬁned and its applica-
tion in clinical problem solving explained to the
students. They then listened to a representative
7 minute audio sample of a self-explanation on a
topic that was not used in the study. They were
then asked to read each case while self-explaining
aloud for 8 minutes and then they had 2 minutes
to write down their diagnosis, together with two
supportive arguments and two plausible alternative
diagnoses. With the students’ consent, their self-
explanations were audio-recorded. The research
assistants, all non-clinicians, prompted students
after any 10 second silence and asked them to
‘please continue to self-explain aloud’. No feed-
back was given on the quality or content of self-
explanations.

DISCUSSION
Several studies from various disciplines have shown
that learners develop a deeper understanding of
instructional materials through self-explanation dur-
ing learning.
8–10 The ﬁrst study on self-explanation
in the context of clinical reasoning replicated these
results.7 This study, which involved medical students
generating self-explanations while solving cases,
resulted 1 week later in a better diagnostic perfor-
mance compared with a control group. This positive
effect was only shown with less familiar cases. In
order to get a better understanding about our initial
ﬁndings, the present study analysed the content of
students’ self-explanation protocols. It aimed to
compare the types of knowledge used by students
diagnosing familiar and less familiar clinical cases
and explored the potential role of biomedical
knowledge in the observed beneﬁt of self-explana-
tion.
The results indicate that a less familiar case stimu-
lates the production of a signiﬁcantly higher num-
ber of self-explanation segments. Unfamiliarity
seems to act as a trigger for students to engage in
more active thinking; the greater diagnostic chal-
lenge encourages them to generate more self-expla-
nations and eventually leads to better learning. This
is in agreement with previous studies showing a
positive relationship between learning and the num-
ber of self-explanations.
8
The total number of inferences generated by stu-
dents is similar for familiar and less familiar cases.
This result contrasts with previous studies showing
that the more inferences the students’ self-explana-
tions contain, the better they learn.
8 However, the
analyses of the two different types of inference, bio-
medical knowledge and clinical knowledge, provide
additional insight into learners’ cognitive mecha-
nisms during self-explanation. When solving less
familiar cases, students generated signiﬁcantly more
biomedical inferences than with familiar cases. Previ-
ous studies have shown that biomedical knowledge
helps students to develop a coherent and stable men-
tal representation of disease, thus enabling them to
retain clinical knowledge over time and to maintain
diagnostic accuracy on challenging cases.
14 Further-
more, studying problems with their underlying
mechanisms in addition to their clinical features,
made students subsequently better able to apply
their knowledge to diagnose unusual cases.
15 Based
on these ﬁndings from the literature, it appears that,
with less familiar cases, self-explanation helps stu-
dents apply biomedical knowledge and create new
links with clinical knowledge. The resulting more
coherent mental representation of disease may then
be retrieved more easily during future diagnostic
problem-solving, allowing for a clearer picture when
the clinical features are uncharacteristic or unorgan-
ised. It is important to note here that in the learning
phase of our ﬁrst study, students who engaged in
self-explanation had received no content-type feed-
back and, thus, without any new external informa-
tion, they must have somehow worked with, and
reorganised, their own prior knowledge.
Previous studies on medical expertise development
have shown that less advanced students use more
biomedical knowledge while solving problems,
12,13
but they did not explore whether an association
existed between this use and learning, i.e. a better
diagnostic performance in future cases. Although
measuring the amount of learning was not part of
the present study, our previous study

showed that self-explanation in the less familiar
cases fostered learning. Therefore, the results of the
present study provide insights into the role of bio-
medical knowledge in learning while solving unfa-
miliar cases with self-explanations. Also, most
studies on medical expertise have used ofﬂine mea-
sures (e.g. free recall) to reconstruct the students’
mental processes. The present study is one of the
few that used an online measure, i.e. the types of
knowledge used by students while solving the cases.
The greater number of errors in less familiar cases,
while few in absolute numbers, probably reﬂects the
fact that speciﬁc knowledge is still being actively
constructed. Moreover, incorrect self-explanations
may foster learning if the student, detecting the
error or misunderstanding after a while, then tries
to resolve it with additional self-explanations. Simi-
larly, the signiﬁcantly increased number of para-
phrases in the less familiar topic may signal that the
students’ speciﬁc knowledge is less elaborate so that
they initially tend to stay closer to the text while
self-explaining. We assume that in the learning
phase, when speciﬁc knowledge is less elaborate,
there may be more room for self-explanation to play
a role in learning.
Self-explanation might be seen not only as a knowl-
edge-building strategy, but also as a reﬂective strat-
egy. Recent studies have shown that internal
medicine residents, who were encouraged to use
structured reﬂection during clinical reasoning, had
better diagnostic accuracy on complex and unusual
cases but not on routine clinical cases.
20 Structured
reﬂection was also recently used as a learning strat-
egy for clerks and compared with generation of an
immediate diagnosis or generation of a differential
diagnosis. In this study, clerks using structured
reﬂection signiﬁcantly outperformed the other two
groups on diagnosing new clinical cases 1 week
later.
6 Self-explanation, although less structured,
might represent an alternative reﬂective approach
for clerks working through their cases.
Some aspects of the present study represent innova-
tions with respect to the growing research literature
on self-explanation. Medical education and clinical
reasoning have been added only recently to the list
of domains for research on self-explanation. Also,
designing appropriate learning material for self-
explanation has recently received much attention
from researchers.
17,21–24 To our knowledge, clinical
cases as the learning material and students’ familiar-
ity with the material as a variable have not been
previously studied. The present study was also a ﬁrst
step to investigate the underlying mechanisms of
self-explanations in clinical reasoning. However, the
limited sample size and the experimental context of
the present study may limit generalisation to the
real clinical learning environment and, hence, more
research is necessary.
The results of this study suggest that, for medical
students at the clerkship level, self-explanation as a
learning strategy for clinical reasoning works better
with less familiar cases because it provides opportu-
nities to link biomedical to clinical knowledge,
which may lead to a coherent representation of dis-
ease. The level of familiarity for students may be an
important issue in designing the appropriate learn-
ing material for self-explanation and clinical reason-
ing. Cases chosen should be challenging enough to
force students to revisit underlying basic biomedical
knowledge. The addition of explicit prompts to that
effect may be useful. Further studies could examine
more directly the evolution of medical knowledge
over time with self-explanation. Also, more studies
are needed to explore self-explanation as a strategy
to enhance reﬂective approaches in clinical
reasoning.

To What Extent Does Nonanalytic Reasoning Contribute
to Visual Learning in Cytopathology?
Andrew Evered, BSc 1,2; Darren Walker, PhD 2; Andrew A. Watt, PhD 2; and and Nick Perham, PhD 2
BACKGROUND: Acquisition of visual interpretation skills in cytopathology may involve 2 strategies. Analytic strategies
require trainees to base their interpretive decisions on carefully considered and often exhaustive cytomorphologic feature
lists, a process that can be time-consuming and inefficient. In contrast, nonanalytic pattern recognition strategies are
rarely encouraged during training, even though this approach is characteristic of expert diagnostic behavior. This study
evaluated the potential role of nonanalytic learning in cytopathology as an efficient alternative to analytic training.
METHODS: Forty-nine cytology novice participants undertook an initial image interpretation test to obtain baseline diag-
nostic accuracy (test 1). Twenty-four participants subsequently received training in basic cervical cytomorphology and
were given a list of cell features for future reference (the “analytic” group). The remaining 25 participants were simply
shown 20 nonannotated paired images of normal and abnormal cervical cells (the “nonanalytic” group). Following a prac-
tice phase, both groups were retested (test 2). Prior to a final test (test 3), participants in both groups were instructed to
adopt a combined analytic/nonanalytic diagnostic strategy. Diagnostic accuracy and response times were measured in
each test. RESULTS: Diagnostic accuracy in both groups improved significantly between tests 1 and 2 ( P<.001) but
decreased between tests 2 and 3 ( P<.05). Speed of response to test images was generally faster under nonanalytic than
under analytic conditions. CONCLUSIONS: Nonanalytic reasoning in cytopathology image interpretation can be as accu-
rate as traditional feature-based reasoning. Encouraging trainees to adopt pattern recognition strategies may help to
expedite the acquisition of visual interpretation skills in cytopathology training programs, yet combining analytic and non-
analytic reasoning do not appear to be effective. Cancer (Cancer Cytopathol) 2013;121:329–38.

KEY WORDS: cytopathology; perceptual learning; pattern recognition; training; cognition.
The primary purpose of cytopathology is to identify cancer cells or their precursors by light microscopy. 1 The
process can be broken down into 3 separate but interdependent problems: visual search for a cellular abnormal-
ity, the recognition of one or more cells as “abnormal” in appearance, and finally, a decision as to whether any
cells are sufficiently atypical to warrant further investigation of the patient. Cutting across each facet is the ques-
tion of how cytologists develop their visual and cognitive skills with training and practice. This question is im-
portant, because visual recognition and classification of abnormal cells is a subjective and error-prone task, even
among highly skilled cytologists.
2,3 Surprisingly little is known about the nature of the visual learning process in
cytopathology, which hinders the development of evidence-based training programs. 4 Training is generally
organized such that novices first learn key cytomorphological features and subsequently perfect their skills dur-
ing a lengthy period of supervised practice.
5,6 However, there is currently no consensus on the appropriate dura-
tion and design of such programs. Evidence-based strategies that minimize costs and demands on staff time may

thology services.7 The current study was motivated by the
dearth of knowledge noted above and by the desire to
formulate a training strategy that might help expedite
the acquisition of visual interpretation skills in cytopa-
thology trainees.
One possible approach to learning visual interpreta-
tion skills is the so-called nonanalytic or “pattern recog-
nition” strategy, which has been widely acknowledged in
the field of radiological image interpretation.
8 Far from
being a new idea, the theoretical basis of this form of rea-
soning came from the philosopher Michael Polanyi in the
1960s, who argued that experienced clinicians possess a
“tacit knowledge” of medicine that cannot be explicitly
expressed and is applied without conscious awareness.
9
His ideas were and still are treated with skepticism by
many clinicians, who hold the contrasting view that clini-
cal judgment is a wholly explicit process deploying ex-
haustive rules and principles.
10–12 Despite its analytic
rigor, rule-based reasoning is costly in terms of its ineffi-
ciency and high demand on working memory resources.
In contrast, rapid nonanalytic perceptual processing of
clinical scenarios appears to be a common trait among
experienced clinicians.
13–15 Moreover, several authors
convincingly argue that an analytic/nonanalytic dichot-
omy is oversimplistic and instead propose that the dual
application of such strategies is more realistic.
16 Dual pro-
cess theory, as it has become known, has found strong
empirical and theoretical support.
17–20
Research spanning more than 30 years strongly sup-
ports the notion that, regardless of the visual domain,
experts adopt more efficient visual processing and
decision-making strategies than do trainees.
21 In cognitive
psychology terms, experts tend to use strategies variably
referred to in the literature as “backward reasoning,”
“similarity-driven reasoning,” or “nonanalytic reasoning,”
in which one or only a small number of tentative diagno-
ses are made from a rapid initial and largely nonanalytic
global impression of the visual scene. This reasoning strat-
egy is highly efficient in its use of short-term memory
resources, and its adoption by experts is generously sup-
ported by research in the fields of radiology, cognitive psy-
chology, and medical decision-making.
22–27 In medical
education, training strategies that include nonanalytic rea-
soning have been shown to enhance the diagnostic per-
formance of novices.
28 It therefore seems curious why
such a tactic is not usually considered in cytopathology
training programs, which, with their emphasis on the de-
velopment of visual interpretation skills, would seem to
be an ideal candidate for such an approach. Instead, cyto-
pathology training usually involves the exhaustive applica-
tion of morphological feature lists and diagnostic “rules,”
all of which must be carefully and systematically consid-
ered before arriving at a diagnosis. The reasons for this
highly analytic strategy are unclear but probably result
from a desire to instill in students a consistent diagnostic
approach and to prevent premature closure and other cog-
nitive biases. As noted above, research in fields other than
cytopathology indicates that analytic and nonanalytic rea-
soning are probably not mutually exclusive processes. A
combination of the 2 seems to be more effective than
either tactic alone,
29–31 an approach that will be tested in
this study.
In light of the uncertainties concerning visual learn-
ing processes and optimum training strategies in cytopa-
thology, the aim of this study was to compare the effect of
rule-based (analytic) training with a nonanalytic “pattern
recognition” style of learning on the subsequent diagnos-
tic performance of novice observers. We hypothesize that
novices who adopt a pure nonanalytic reasoning strategy
can achieve levels of diagnostic accuracy equal to that
achieved using a purely analytic approach. In addition, we
propose that novices instructed to adopt a combination of
nonanalytic and analytic reasoning achieve diagnostic
accuracy greater than those instructed to emphasize either
tactic alone.
To operationalize the 2 approaches to visual learn-
ing, we have adopted what is commonly referred to as
“alternative forced choice” methodology.
32 The most
common form of this type of experiment is the 2-alterna-
tive forced choice experiment in which an observer exam-
ines 2 images simultaneously, only one of which is
abnormal. The observer indicates which image is abnor-
mal, and the data are analyzed to determine the percent-
age of correct decisions. An important drawback of
alternative forced choice experiments is their lack of eco-
logical validity: the method does not resemble an actual
clinical paradigm. However, several studies suggest that
variants of this technique can successfully enhance the vis-
ual learning process in novice dermatologists and histopa-
thologists and may therefore be a useful training tool.
33–36

employed, studies of visual diagnostic performance
require some measure of accuracy or error as the
